Teams seeking short-term help or insurance behind center should have targeted previous Cards QB2 Gardner Minshew II (something we telegraphed with foresight). Now Brissett could be such an alternative – though Sunday's remarkable win at Dallas was a reminder that Minshew was the cheaper alternative with more upside. Any team trading for the statuesque Brissett – who has 73 mostly unremarkable NFL starts on his resume – would have to pick up the remainder of his $9.7 million base salary, which is more than three times new QB1 Minshew's base compensation. Given Brissett was just demoted to third string in the desert, the better approach might be to wait and see if he's released after the deadline.

He can set an edge effectively and hunt passers, whether deployed in three- or four-man fronts. Sweat, 29, made a case to be the MVP of Super Bowl 60 for the Eagles after collecting 2½ sacks of Patrick Mahomes in Philly's blowout of the Kansas City Chiefs. The 6-5, 265-pounder is now in the second season of a four-year, $76.4 million deal with the struggling Cardinals but has no guaranteed money beyond 2026. He could be the final piece for a team looking to put a cherry on top of a championship-caliber (or championship-adjacent) defense. And his play has been picking up, Sweat collecting three sacks and 16 QB pressures over the past five games, according to Next Gen Stats.

The Ravens, who play Thursday, could be facing some existential decisions – as far as football rosters go – in the coming days. Currently 4-4 and potentially without QB Lamar Jackson for the remainder of the season, GM Eric DeCosta and Co. might have to take a hard look at their options this weekend given no team is more overspent in 2027 − nearly $46 million in the red on next year's salary cap, per Over The Cap. Jackson's inability to stay on the field, to say nothing of the $84.3 million cap number he'll carry into 2027, his final year under contract, also make it worth wondering if Baltimore may conclude it's time to cut ties with a player who's also been difficult to negotiate new deals with. What is fairly clear is that Henry, 32, isn't nearly as effective – or as frequently used – when Jackson isn't in the lineup. But his tank also obviously isn't empty and offloading his $11 million salary in 2027 might be the right play for Baltimore while helping a team looking to pay something less than the Jonathan Taylor price for running back help.

While the Browns fell to third place in the AFC North over the weekend, they're still only one game back of the division-leading Pittsburgh Steelers. Yet Jeudy, a seventh-year vet with 16 catches this season, doesn't appear to be a significant part of Cleveland's current offense … or future plans. He signed a three-year, $52.5 million extension two years ago and responded with his first Pro Bowl effort in 2024. But Jeudy's production essentially fell by 50% in 2025 (50 catches, 602 yards, two TDs) amid the team's unsettled QB situation, and he's fallen into further disuse this year – when the Browns chose wideouts in the first (KC Concepcion Jr.) and second (Denzel Boston) rounds of the draft. A change of scenery could make sense and moving Jeudy, 27, shouldn't be especially difficult given he has no guaranteed money beyond this year.

Trading a player who had nearly 1,500 receiving yards in 2025 is admittedly a stretch – especially since the Cowboys, even if they lose again this weekend at Indianapolis, still wouldn't be hopelessly out of the NFC East race. And yet coach Brian Schottenheimer has been openly critical of Pickens, who hasn't been living up to the $27.3 million cost of his franchise tag this season. Most teams aren't even in financial position to pick up the remainder of that tab. But it only takes one buyer willing to roll the dice on a sublime talent – and owner Jerry Jones' willingness to let Pickens go two months earlier than he probably will anyway – for something to come together quickly, especially if the Cowboys can get a better return than the compensatory draft pick they'd likely get in 2028 if Pickens signs elsewhere next March.

More: Jerry Jones calls Cowboys' collapse vs. Cardinals 'an indictment'

From a contractual standpoint, the disappointing Texans couldn't move some of their top veterans if they wanted to. Clowney doesn't fall into that category. He's also 33 and would likely require a fairly defined role elsewhere, though he's thrived as something of a mercenary in the latter stages of his career. And dealing a $2.5 million base salary is a cinch if a suitor willing to take it emerges.

No player is generating more interest or speculation as the deadline nears. And why not given the Colts are actively dismantling their roster following Ballard's ouster, and Taylor is the rare player who can join a new team and make an immediate difference? Through 92 career NFL games over six-plus seasons, he's averaged 107.4 yards and nearly a TD from scrimmage per appearance – rare impact that's rarely available. And if you're thinking Taylor, 27, shouldn't be available after signing a two-year, $44 million extension in August, think again. The Colts would only take a $10 million cap hit next year if they deal him given he has no guarantees in either 2027 or 2028.

None would generate nearly the return of draft capital – nor help ameliorate the Gardner trade – in the manner that Taylor that might. But this trio are all on expiring contracts and could provide valuable depth, if not patch a lineup, for a contender. Downs has already expressed a desire to leave, though crafty vets like Allen and Stewart might be more optimal rentals.

He's two years removed from being a first-round pick, 23rd overall in 2024, and a massive statistical output as a rookie (87 catches for 1,282 yards and 10 TDs). But Thomas' production was effectively cut in half last year, the Jags' first under head coach Liam Coen, and it's plummeted even further this season. Currently operating as basically the fifth wideout, now that CB/WR Travis Hunter seems to be getting more heavily involved in the offense again, it sure seems like Thomas could benefit from a fresh start – and his contract should allow for it.

While first-round picks have fully guaranteed pacts, the bulk of them are paid as signing bonuses, leaving the base salaries as manageable. Thomas is making $1.075 million this season and is due $2.8 million in 2027. His fifth-year option would effectively serve as a balloon payment in 2028, but that will be picked up − or declined − by whomever Thomas is playing for next spring. A deal would mean Jacksonville's cap hit in 2027 wouldn't even be $2 million, while an acquiring team would find itself with some options even if a two-month audition with Thomas doesn't turn out optimally.

The winless Bolts have yet to show any sign of surrender despite an 0-7 record that's looked as ugly as it would indicate.

Even at 35, Mack, a nine-time Pro Bowler and former Defensive Player of the Year, remains a force in this league – one who's in the year-to-year portion of his career and unsigned for 2027. And given his age, he might not cost as much to obtain as a player like Sweat – particularly for a team that might be all in for the short run only. Tuipulotu is also on an expiring contract, though the 24-year-old might be tougher to pry away – especially if the Chargers deem him worthy of the franchise tag next year, if not an outright extension.

Johnston, a 6-2, 208 pounder drafted in the first round three years ago, has compelling tools but has also struggled with drops and hasn't been productive in Mike McDaniel's offense, though he's hardly alone. And a fully guaranteed $18 million salary in 2027 could make him a tough sell.

The rebooting Fins certainly don't need to be in the business of parting with potential foundational players. With four sacks and 34 pressures in six games, Robinson, a first-round pick in 2024 – before the current regime was hired this year – is in the midst of his best season, which makes the 23-year-old an intriguing target. But his age, trajectory and position could make the asking price prohibitive.

He's thrown 12 TD passes against three interceptions, has averaged nearly 240 passing yards per game and owns a career-best 104.5 passer rating – far superior numbers than he posted with the Las Vegas Raiders in 2025 and more in line with his Pro Bowl years in Seattle. The Jets are also 2-6, and Smith, 36, is playing on an expiring contract with a $3.3 million base salary − as if it wasn't already obvious he's not part of the bigger blueprint here. Also, can a team like the Minnesota Vikings afford not to inquire about him?

Is he the Jets' best offensive player? Probably. Do they seem likely to part with him, too? It wouldn't seem so, but Wilson, a fifth-year vet who's only 26, has clashed with Smith and coach Aaron Glenn at times amid this franchise's ongoing struggle to achieve relevance. Like Gardner, Wilson signed a four-year extension a year ago – and like Gardner's pact, the base salaries are high, meaning it's not a very difficult contract to move. If GM Darren Mougey gets another godfather offer for a player who could make all the difference − and for an extended period − in a place like San Francisco, Atlanta or elsewhere, he'd certainly have to listen ... particularly given the progress shown by fellow Jets WRs Omar Cooper Jr. and Mitchell.

Will EVP/GM Howie Roseman embrace the rare the opportunity to be a seller, even with the NFC East still in reach? It's hard to see Philly doing much in the playoffs even if they somehow retain the division crown. Baun's been a Pro Bowler the past two seasons and has an excellent nose for the ball. But Roseman would need a compelling offer to part with a player under contract in 2027 and who would generate a $22.3 million dead cap hit in 2027 if he's dealt.

Now in his walk year in Nashville – and at a time when the floundering Titans clearly aren't going anywhere, especially after letting Simmons go – Pollard is working on a fifth straight season with more than 1,000 yards rushing and has averaged 42 receptions over the previous four years. He's also got a hot hand with 292 yards and five TDs from scrimmage over the past two weeks. A pretty good dual threat and one only owed the prorated amount of his $6.7 million base salary this season.

Johnson, a first-round pick of the Jets in 2022, is also coming on with two sacks and 11 pressures over the past three games. Also headed for free agency in 2027, the former Pro Bowler could be a nice near-term addition to any pass rush rotation.

#2770. Josh Jacobs needs to display more (or any) contrition

In May 2026, Packers running back Josh Jacobs crossed a line that should never be crossed. And neither he nor his representatives are acting accordingly in what should be an effort to seek redemption.

He pleaded no contest to battery of a woman. He’s fighting in court to keep the video secret. He’s responding to additional allegations through a strident statement from his lawyers attacking the accusers.

The most tone-deaf gesture of all came last Thursday night, when he celebrated a touchdown by pretending to wear, and to be released from, handcuffs.

His implausible explanation, which accused Prime Video of not showing enough of the celebration and attacked the media for interpreting the images with their lyin’ eyes, was contradicted by the full video of the event.

That’s not the way to play this. His no-contest plea is equivalent to saying, “I did it.” He should be contrite. He should be apologetic. He should be seeking redemption.

The Packers continue to stand behind him, primarily because he’s the best running back on the roster and they want to win games. Their reported interest in Colts running back Jonathan Taylor strongly suggests that, if the Packers could get Taylor, the support for Jacobs would immediately evaporate.

Here’s the basic reality. If the Packers were to cut Jacobs, would anyone sign him? The Chiefs took plenty of heat last week for adding kicker Justin Tucker to the practice squad; they may not be inclined to give another second chance to a player whose arrival would compound the negative reaction to Tucker’s arrival.

The reality, in every sport at every level, is obvious. If the player has enough skill and ability, someone will find a way to justify behavior that shouldn’t be tolerated by an industry that relies so heavily on support from the public, both directly through ticket sales and TV ratings and indirectly through taxpayer funding for stadium projects.

Still, Jacobs has done himself no favors by adopting a posture of defiance. He did something no man should ever do. He’s lucky he’s good enough at football to not lose his job over it.

If he was at the bottom of the depth chart in Green Bay, he would have been gone a long time ago.

#2766. 2026 season could highlight the unfairness of the eight-division structure

From time to time, the NFL’s current structure has created unfair results, with the best of four bad teams assigned to a predetermined division earning a playoff berth and the home game that goes along with it.

This year, the NFC has two very strong divisions, one so-so division, and one very weak division.

Here’s the basic reality. With the four NFC division winners getting tickets to the playoff party, the wild-card berths will go to three teams. And, currently, there are three teams in the NFC North and two in the NFC West that are potentially better than whoever will win the NFC East and the NFC South.

Between the Vikings, Bears, Lions, Packers, 49ers, Seahawks, and Rams, two will be crowned division winners. That leaves five for the wild-card berths.

Ultimately, two of them will be frozen out of the playoffs — even if both of those teams end up with better records than the best teams of the NFC East and NFC South.

During last Friday’s episode of PFT Live, I threw out an alternative approach that would be far more fair to all teams.

Instead of two conferences with a quartet of four-team divisions, why not pivot to four eight-team divisions?

NFL East, NFL North, NFL South, NFL West. The easiest configuration would consist of slapping the current East, North, South, and West divisions into one conference each. While some tweaks could be needed to better align things geographically, it would be far more fair to guarantee a playoff spot (and a home game) to the best of eight teams, not the best of four teams.

Decisions would have to be made about scheduling. The home-and-home series (a vestige of the days when there were far fewer teams) would need to be retired. Each team would play the seven other teams in its conference, with 10 (or 11, inevitably) other games.

The playoffs would consist of the four conference champions (with the best two getting byes) and 10 wild-card teams. And there would be an added benefit — it would be possble to have the best two teams meet in the Super Bowl, without regard to the traditional AFL-NFL/AFC-NFC separation.

It would be one league. One playoff tree. Any combination of teams would, in theory, be possible for the Super Bowl. When the dust settles on the semifinal round, the best two teams would remain.

That said, it won’t be easy to get the owners to give up the current format, which entails in any given year a one-in-four shot at hosting a playoff game. But if the goal is to constantly strive for ways to create more compelling matchups, an eight-team, four-conference approach makes a lot more sense than the current structure.

Football is a meritocracy. A configuration of four, eight-team conferences would be far more conducive to that ideal.

Will it happen? Probably not. Should it be taken seriously by the league? Absolutely.

Maybe this year, when the NFC East and NFC South provide none-of-the-above champions and two very viable teams are sent home after Week 18, will spark a real conversation about meaningful change.

#2761. Bryce Young, C.J. Stroud continue fourth seasons without new contracts

Several players taken in the first round of the 2023 NFL draft have gotten their second contracts. The first two players picked that year still have not.

Halfway through their fourth seasons, Panthers quarterback Bryce Young and Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud continue to play under their rookie deals.

As to Stroud, a subpar third season complicated negotiations. A decision was made to proceed with his fourth season, without a second deal.

A Tuesday article from ESPN took a close look at the respective preseason positions of player and team. The key facts: (1) the Texans offered a contract with a new-money value in excess of $50 million; and (2) Stroud did not ask to be the highest-paid quarterback in the league. (Patrick Mahomes currently leads the way at $63.093 million.)

Although the Texans have slumped to 2-5 in 2026, Stroud’s play has improved significantly. A new deal — closer to the top of the market — becomes likely after the current season. It remains theoretically possible that the two sides could work something out sooner than that.

For the player, there’s always an urgency to shift the injury risk to the team. Especially when the player will be assuming 60 minutes of injury risk, 17 times over.

As to Young, we’ve recently caught wind of chatter that the Panthers are “far down the road” toward signing him to a second deal in excess of $50 million per year.

Both are under contract through 2027, with their fifth-year options already exercised. For both, the guaranteed salary in 2027 will be $25.904 million. The franchise tag becomes an option for 2028, absent new deals.

Most teams prefer to make a final decision before then. Up or out. New contract, or find a new quarterback.

Again, both Young and Stroud are eligible for new contracts at any time. Both teams seem to want to keep them around. The only questions at this are when the deals will be one, what the new-money value will be, and (most importantly) how the payments will be structured — especially as to guarantees.

#2756. Doom and Gloom: Overreactions to Utah’s slow start to the 2026-27 season

This has not gone as well as we had hoped. Seven games into the season, and all that the "winning time" Utah Jazz are bringing to show and tell is a solitary one-point win against a subpar New Orleans team and a head bowed in shame. It was a depressing show-and-tell presentation for this premature Jazz team.

But growing pains are part of the deal. Winning in the NBA isn't as simple as a change in mindset; it's a change in identity. A fundamental shift in the direction of a franchise will take time to set, especially one as drastic as going from hunting the number-one overall lottery odds to walking the thorn-riddled path toward the Western Conference playoffs.

Just as Michael Scott learned that it takes much more than shouting in the office to declare bankruptcy, Utah is learning firsthand that flipping the "winning" switch is much harder than simply making a declaration. The Jazz wanted and expected to win many more basketball games this season; they clearly still have some growing up to do before they can reach that switch.

Still, it wasn't ridiculous to expect more from this team by now. They traded for Jaren Jackson Jr., one of the best front-court defenders in basketball and a multiple-time All-Star, to pair alongside Utah's in-house All-Star, Lauri Markkanen. They drafted Darryn Peterson, a player touted as one of the best guard prospects in recent memory and a future star. They re-signed Keyonte George, rewarding him for his steady growth and remarkable leadership.

But 1-6 is 1-6, and the Utah Jazz are way off course at this larval moment in the 2026-27 season. Not all is lost, but much needs evaluation and careful reconsideration. So let's play a game that I like to call "Doom and Gloom". The rules are simple: I'll share an opinion that I've thought myself or heard from others about Utah's unsettling beginning and determine whether said opinion is "Doom", a bad omen and an imminent issue, or "Gloom", an overreaction that, while based in reality, doesn't tell the whole story.

SAN ANTONIO, TX – NOVEMBER 2: Ace Bailey #19 of the Utah Jazz drives to the basket during the game against the San Antonio Spurs on November 2, 2026 at Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Adam Hagy/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

No, the Utah Jazz are not winning basketball games. Yes, that is a massive problem, and a legitimate cause for concern for a team whose goal is to win basketball games.

But this problem, as with all others, deserves some context before it stirs up panic.

The biggest factor, I believe, is the Jazz's strength of competition. According to ESPN's RPI, the Jazz are tied at number-one for the hardest schedule in the entire NBA. They've faced the reigning Western Conference champions, San Antonio, twice while the Spurs were at full strength. Who could have foreseen the Memphis Grizzlies, who Utah faced twice, starting the season at 6-1? In fact, all the teams that beat the Jazz at this point of the season are a collective 22-6.

Despite the majority of this Jazz core having played together for years, this is a team still discovering itself. Give them time.

Injury luck has not flipped in Utah's favor early — five big men have been injured at some point in the season — but to blame their shortcomings on injuries is disingenuous.

Jusuf Nurkic hasn't been available since the first game of the preseason, Jaxon Hayes went down with an injury against Los Angeles, and then Markkanen and JJJ went down in the same half against Memphis. Markkanen and Hayes returned quickly, but shortly thereafter Mo Bamba — who has been unironically excellent — rolled his ankle in San Antonio.

That's bad luck, and Utah will obviously underperform without their best players on the court. But playoff-caliber teams regroup and find ways to win while shorthanded. If the Jazz can't win while JJJ recovers from his MCL injury, their playoff chances were slim from the start.

Alright, it's time for some therapeutic pessimism. On the topic of Utah's young players, I have to be painfully honest: Utah's tanking-fueled draft yield has been tragic.

Let's look at the Jazz's body of work in terms of draft picks. Of their four lottery picks, only two are still on Utah's roster. First to leave was Taylor Hendricks, who spends his days at the end of Memphis' bench and doesn't appear likely to sign an extension at the end of the season. It's a similar story for Cody Williams, who, despite generating plenty of preseason static in Minnesota, has appeared in five games and scored zero points.

Utah traded up to pick Florida star Walter Clayton Jr. last year, and he's already on his third NBA team.

As for the draftees still on Utah's roster, Isaiah Collier's team option was just declined, and Kyle Filipowski hardly sees the court even as injuries pile up in Will Hardy's frontcourt rotation.

Sensabaugh's minutes have been uneven, but he's filled his role well and had the trust of his head coach to replace Darryn Peterson in the lineup when their first clash with San Antonio entered overtime. Still, his status with the team is uncertain as he approaches the final year of his contract.

That list doesn't inspire much optimism, but it isn't all bad in terms of the youth of Utah.

Keyonte George has been excellent this year, with the exception of a stinker against San Antonio. Ace Bailey is a revelation, making winning plays with and without the basketball, playing stellar defense, and becoming an offensive rebound magnet. And Darryn Peterson, despite looking uneven out of the gate (more on this later), has still shown flashes of what makes him such an enticing prospect.

Semi-Doom is a bit of a cop-out, I'll admit. But there's still reason to believe in Utah's young core, even if the majority of their swings have inarguably whiffed.

Even worse than seeing Utah lose five consecutive games is seeing how the team has responded to adversity.

Without a rallying cry or an increased sense of urgency, this team is full of players with no experience winning at an NBA level. They haven't been able to hit that next gear, and the team mopes on the court, on the sideline, and in timeouts.

This is all about perception, so I might be out of line, but winners turn losing streaks into winning streaks. Utah is giving its fanbase little reason to expect a turnaround because they don't appear to expect one themselves.

Being a guard in the NBA is incredibly difficult, and development isn't linear.

What we're seeing in Peterson isn't a lack of basketball talent, ability, or confidence. In fact, he's displayed all three of those qualities in droves in his young career. Instead, we're observing the metamorphosis of a college star into an NBA-level player. Darryn Peterson joins a Utah Jazz team where he is the fourth offensive option behind Markkanen, George, and Jackson Jr. Finding his place in the rotation and getting accustomed to his new circumstances was bound to bring growing pains.

The biggest concern has been his lack of athletic burst and top-end speed, keeping him away from the basket. Instead, he's sustained himself on a diet of floaters and mid-range jumpers, while getting comfortable with a quick-trigger three-point shot.

For every poetic dribble combo leading into a buttery-smooth jumper, Peterson is due for a forced off-balance fling. He's playing in the big leagues, which means the competition is bigger, stronger, and faster than he's ever faced.

And I'm still highly encouraged by what he's displayed to this point. The jumper looks slick, comfortable, and will find its target with greater consistency over time. Keyonte was a sub-40% shooter from the field as a rookie; he shot 45.6% in his third year.

Alright, I'll wave the red flag for this one. Utah's offense has been abhorrent this season, and we can't blame tanking on their ratings anymore.

Currently possessing the 29th-ranked offense in the entire NBA, the Jazz have scored under 100 points in their last two games. Lauri Markkanen played in both of those games and has performed well beneath his standard. At just 16.5 points per game, the player who has been Utah's offensive pillar and averaged over 26 points per game a season ago is shooting below 40% from the field.

Against San Antonio on Monday, Markkanen and Peterson were the only Jazz players to score in double digits.

The absence of Jusuf Nurkic has been devastating to Will Hardy's offensive game plan. Heavily reliant on ball screens and passing from the center position, Jaxon Hayes simply isn't the playmaker this system requires to succeed. Nor are Mo Bamba or Tony Bradley.

Having to adjust on the fly, the Jazz offense has been clunky, ineffective, and overly dependent on self-creation to pose any real threat. Either one player's injury has truly been that catastrophic to Utah's offensive integrity, or Will Hardy is struggling to conjure up an alternative play style. Either way, none of this is good.

Calvin Barrett is the Associate Editor for SLC Dunk and a Utah Jazz columnist for the Standard-Examiner. Originally from Springville, Utah, he currently writes from his desk in Japan.

#2750. 2027 NFL mock draft has major QB changes throughout first round

A 2027 NFL Draft class that once looked to be rife with star power is suddenly sparking a good deal of mystery at the top of the first round.

That uncertainty starts, of course, with the quarterbacks. With Texas' Arch Manning floundering in the early season before finding steadier ground in recent weeks and Oregon's Dante Moore now out for the season, there's no clear pecking order for the top passers.

But with several teams facing pressure to replace their incumbent starting signal-callers, the demand for solutions behind center isn't likely to wane anytime soon.

Here's our latest first-round projection, using ESPN's current average draft position for each team to establish a first-round order:

For as transcendent a talent as Smith is, it's no sure thing that he becomes the first receiver since Keyshawn Johnson in 1996 to be taken first overall. Still, with no quarterback having established himself as clearly worthy of the top spot, the case is getting stronger for the Ohio State star to land here. Cam Ward is finally showing some encouraging signs of growth, though it remains clear that he's not getting nearly enough help from his receiving corps. Smith could change that in a hurry by giving the No. 1 pick someone who can be trusted to come down with deep heaves.

It takes a truly special cornerback to be selected No. 2 overall, which is as high as any other cornerback has gone in the modern draft era. Moore sure seems like he shapes up as exactly that, though. A true lockdown presence in coverage, the 6-2, 197-pound cover man changes the way a defense functions, as teams wholesale avoid testing him. In joining 2026 first-rounder Chris Johnson, Moore would help Jeff Hafley get this build off the ground floor.

This move might only be in play if the Chargers part ways with Tuli Tuipulotu, with whom the team couldn't reach agreement on a long-term extension this summer. Yet Los Angeles will need to confront its precipitous fall from the contending class, and it's not out of the question that the team might balk at his price tag. Stewart's singular explosiveness as an edge rusher could compel teams to look past his on-field blow-ups, and he could take his place as a much-needed cornerstone for the Bolts.

Amid a full-scale collapse of what Howie Roseman so carefully built over the years, the Eagles have resisted drastic in-season change. But in one form or another, an overhaul looks inevitable next offseason. Perhaps Roseman doesn't want to rush a quarterback decision while facing that terrain. But it might also be difficult for him to bypass the opportunity to truly turn the page on what's a bygone era as Jalen Hurts' future remains clouded. Even as the front-runner to be the first passer chosen, Mestemaker still has considerable room to grow – and he might even end up a 2028 prospect rather than a '27 one. Nevertheless, he's the kind of centerpiece who could make a rebuild much more palatable.

In a class in which more physically gifted passers have largely faded in the early season, Carr figures to be a quarterback who could have staying power. His advanced feel for reading defenses and consistently clean mechanics allow him to keep his offense on schedule, which NFL teams will surely admire. Pedestrian physical tools and a play-it-safe style might leave some wondering about his ceiling, but predictable efficiency at quarterback is something the Jets would likely leap at.

No longer just the clear-cut choice as the No. 1 linebacker in this class, Cole has positioned himself to be considered in the top tier of defenders. As teams shift to a heavier dose of under-center looks, the 6-3, 235-pounder is exactly the type of countermeasure capable of snuffing out big plays before they get started. He'd be a boon to a Jets defense that might be at an impasse until it collects more top-tier young talent.

Ranking 31st in both rushing EPA per play allowed and pressure rate, according to Next Gen Stats, New Orleans has a clear problem that starts up front. Echoles is the kind of do-everything defensive lineman who could transform the landscape of Brandon Staley's group.

Between the potential for the team to miss out on a top-five pick and the sudden scarcity of top-tier quarterback options, Arizona could end up in a no-man's land for draft options behind center – at least in the early going. Rather than force the issue, the Cardinals might be wise to simply nab a blue-chip talent at another premium position. Simmons' pass-rush prowess is unmatched at the college level, and his persistence and power in stuffing the run have made him a complete edge defender.

After hitting it big with this year's Sonny Styles pick, the Commanders would really stand to benefit from another immediate contributor in a vulnerable secondary. Like Styles, Hampton is a supersized player (6-2, 205 pounds) at his position who regularly exerts his will against the opposition. He could use a dose of Styles' restraint when trying to blanket receivers, but he's a thoroughly frustrating matchup for any pass catcher to take on.

The Falcons have long had a formidable collection of skill-position talent, but it's long felt as though the passing attack has been missing another piece. Becker would make for a lethal deep tandem with Drake London, who's carrying a disproportionate load in the receiving corps, and help give Atlanta a clearer sense of whether Michael Penix Jr. is the franchise's quarterback of the future.

Turning the page on Lamar Jackson just days after his thumb injury might seem premature. But with the two-time NFL MVP holding all the cards in contract negotiations necessitating some resolution this offseason, it feels as though Baltimore could be staring down the end of an era. If the Ravens do part with Jackson, the team could try to bring on another scintillating offensive catalyst in Chambliss. The stocky signal-caller's track record of turning things up a notch in crunch time against top competition should endear him to NFL decision-makers, and his comfort attacking the middle of the field should assuage any concerns about his height.

Game-changing defensive tackles don't come cheap. But if the Raiders want to jolt a defense that's surrendered 30 or more points in five consecutive games, getting a true difference-maker along the line might be the best route to do so. With six sacks on the season, Gilliam has shown he can be a mainstay in opposing backfields.

The protection plan for Bryce Young has come undone, with the quarterback taking 11 sacks in the last two weeks. Getting back on the right track might require a fresh start up front. Seaton's quickness as a pass blocker sets him apart from other offensive tackles in this class, making him a suitable partner to work opposite 2026 first-round pick Monroe Freeling.

A double-dip on Georgia defenders probably isn't a bad call for a unit hurting for playmakers, particularly on the back end. Though Robinson still has to master the finer points of his position, he boasts the requisite size, speed and ball skills to stick with top-flight receivers and make quarterbacks pay for testing him.

Despite his remarkably efficient start to the season, Mensah likely still has more to prove against much more formidable competition before he can cement a place in the first tier of quarterbacks. If he doesn't waver down the stretch, however, Mensah might be an attractive choice for a team that can look past his so-so arm strength and athleticism and instead build an offense around his precision. He might make particular sense for a Browns team that can't maximize its young offensive pieces until it turns the reins over to a more decisive passer.

General manager Nick Caserio said last week he's at a loss for why Houston's offensive line continues to be so problematic for the rest of the unit. With more swings necessary to address the issue, Williams certainly sizes up as one of the more appealing options. Though he's still coming into his own in his first year as a starter, the 6-8, 305-pound blocker has displayed the kind of rapid growth that has vaulted him into the Day 1 discussion.

John Harbaugh casting a net for Jeffery Simmons shows just how interested the Giants are in recapturing a highly disruptive defensive lineman. That effort in the draft could continue with Stone. Production still lags well behind potential when assessing the 6-3, 312-pounder, whose stock could slide if he doesn't display more consistency down the stretch. Nevertheless, there likely will be no shortage of coaching staffs eager to coax out the best of him.

Though Tristan Wirfs and Luke Goedeke remain bookend tackles for Tampa Bay, a shaky interior line has only increased the volatility of the Buccaneers' offense. Johnson could be this year's Vega Ioane as a potential top-20 pick who can solidify the guard spot in a hurry for whichever team drafts him.

Taking a running back this early might be a non-starter to a Browns front office that doesn't prioritize the position in its investment approach. Still, Cleveland will have to ensure the ask of its next quarterback isn't too great, and improving a rushing attack that ranks 29th in expected points added per rush has to be a consideration.

Even though Jaxon Smith-Njigba has proven more than up to the task of carrying the Seahawks' offense, it's unreasonable to count on him to maintain such a heavy workload and blistering pace. Explosive plays are vital to Seattle's attack, and Coleman can provide them. His erratic play has left some questions about whether he can be trusted to be a true top target, but Sam Darnold can make the most of his skill set as a downfield weapon.

The George Pickens marriage appears to be fizzling out. With everything looking so difficult for an offense that was supposed to propel the team, Dallas might be due for a substantial change. Marsh is hardly a one-for-one replacement for Pickens, but his competitive flair would strike a sharp contrast with a pass catcher whose subpar run-blocking efforts were called out by coach Brian Schottenheimer.

Grappling with the likes of Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins is never fun for opponents. That's the Steelers' reality for the foreseeable future, however, and sending off Joey Porter Jr. only complicates that task. At 6-4 and 205 pounds, Jones combines the size to pester both well-built receivers and the speed to stick close by each one.

The Patriots are riding out their one-year trial period with Kevin Byard, but an offseason pivot from the 33-year-old ballhawk might be necessary. Aggressive yet heady, Bolden is an extremely Mike Vrabel-coded defender. His versatility and range would afford defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr a good deal of schematic flexibility.

Bypassing a cornerback here might be seen by many as malpractice. But Lions general manager Brad Holmes has never been one to be boxed in by positional constraints, and it seems unlikely he'd stray from his ways with the top options in the secondary already accounted for. If Sam LaPorta's contract talks with Detroit reach a breaking point, Johnson could offer the offense a path forward, as Jared Goff would surely come to appreciate his reliability over the middle.

With his season cut short by a concussion, Moore figures to be one of the most perplexing evaluations of a draft class now riddled with questions at quarterback. While some teams might be reticent to invest heavily in the 6-3, 220-pound passer, Minnesota might make plenty of sense for him. The Kyler Murray experiment is becoming untenable, which could leave Kevin O'Connell and Co. back at square one this offseason. And though expecting to find a signal-caller capable of steering a contender might be a dicey proposition for a team likely to select on the back end of Day 1, Moore can be a deft distributor in an offense that affords him plenty of weapons.

Equipping Patrick Mahomes with at least one true threat at receiver might seem like the overwhelming top priority for an offense that has hit a wall in its two-game skid. But between Josh Simmons' inability to stay on the field and Jaylon Moore being on the final year of his deal, Kansas City is approaching a dangerous place on the future of its offensive line. A driving force behind Kentucky's surge this season, Heard has barreled into the first-round conversation with his punishing play.

No coach covets a jumbo Joker like Sean Payton does. The 6-7, 237-pound Green, who missed four games due to a knee injury, hasn't been the dominant force some envisioned him becoming this season. But NFL coaches will relish the opportunity to deploy one of the more imposing pass catchers to come through the college ranks in several years. Green could help provide Bo Nix with some simple solutions as a reliable weapon on contested catches, and his big-play potential could invigorate an attack that's too often settled for a methodical approach.

A rebooted defense already faced offseason uncertainty on the back end due to the expiring contracts of cornerbacks DJ Turner II and Dax Hill. Now, the secondary's instability has threatened to impede the progress of a unit capable of supporting Joe Burrow and Co. when the pass rush is clicking. At 6-0 and 203 pounds, McClain isn't the physical marvel that Duke Tobin tends to gravitate toward, but the former cornerback closes in on the ball in a hurry and has made great strides with his ball production (two interceptions, five passes defensed).

With its defense nearly devoid of true building blocks after the Jeffery Simmons trade, Tennessee will be under great scrutiny as it tries to supercharge the unit. Far more nimble than his 6-5, 300-pound build might suggest, Thompkins has shown considerable potential in a breakout season at Alabama. Though he might not measure up to Simmons on his own – few players do – Thompkins still could give Robert Saleh a figure around which to construct a fresh front.

DaVon Hamilton being lost for the season to a torn quadriceps muscle only further heightens the odds of Jacksonville fully resetting on the interior next year. Wrecking shop at the line of scrimmage shouldn't be a problem for Washington, who can create favorable looks for others and blow up the line of scrimmage when he doesn't draw a double-team.

Medical concerns continue to cloud the stock of Viliamu-Asa, who has torn his anterior cruciate ligament twice and missed time this year with a thumb injury. But if the Bills are comfortable with his outlook, he could be the kind of rangy and versatile presence at the second level that's necessary to help put this unit on more stable ground.

The best teams afford themselves the luxury of thinking ahead. Trent Williams said this summer that 2027 will likely be his last season, which could allow for a smooth succession plan if San Francisco wants to enact one. The prospect of using a first-round pick on a player coming off a torn patellar tendon might alarm a fan base rattled by rampant injuries, but Goosby might be too promising of a protector to pass up if he slides this far.

Despite Michael Olise and Manuel Neuer both taking part in Bayern Munich's final training session ahead of Tuesday's Champions League away clash against Atletico Madrid, it remains unclear whether – and to what extent – either player will feature.

Eberl also stressed Bayern's determination to return to winning ways in the Champions League after drawing their last two games in the competition, while acknowledging how difficult it is to come away with a positive result on the road against Atletico Madrid.

“It’s a top Champions League fixture. We need to show resilience right now. We must keep going if we want to win major titles, and that’s what we want. We want to win in Madrid. The points we dropped in Stavanger are still hanging over us; tomorrow we have a chance to make amends," he said.

“It’s definitely one of the trickiest away fixtures you can face in the Champions League, against opponents who are extremely tough to play against and possess a very high standard of quality, where we’ll have to bring to the game the resilience we’ve had to demonstrate over the past few weeks. #2747. Jalen Brunson has a simple explanation for his surprisingly slow Knicks start

Jalen Brunson's field goal percentage (39.3 percent), 3-point percentage (33.3 percent) and free-throw percentage (73.2 percent) are all significantly down from last year. In fact, the field goal and 3-point percentage would represent the worst of his career, while the free-throw percentage would be second worst.

The Knicks captain has uncharacteristically been misfiring.

There isn't some deep-lying issue or explanation, though. Brunson believes it's actually quite simple.

"Missing shots," Brunson said after practice Tuesday, "I normally make."

New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson reacts after making a 3-point shot against the Brooklyn Nets on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, at Madison Square Garden in New York. JASON SZENES FOR NEW YORK POST

Brunson's shooting was always a worry after he underwent surgery to fix a tendon issue in his left wrist during the offseason. He spoke before the season about how it disrupted his normal offseason workouts and caused him to take way fewer shots than he normally does.

It is certainly understandable that there is early-season rust. But, true to his character, he refused to use that excuse.

"Not at all," Brunson said when asked how much the surgery has affected his early-season form.

His shot diet, in terms of the percentage of pullups vs. catch-and-shoot and shot distance, is similar to last season's. As are the percentages of open shots vs. tightly covered shots. This is not a case of worse shot quality leading to worse results.

There is one area in which there has been a big drop, though. He is struggling in what is usually his specialty.

Brunson's efficiency at the end of the shot clock is way down. He is shooting just 26.7 percent with between 7 and 4 seconds left on the shot clock and 35.7 percent with under four seconds left. Last year, he was at 48.8 percent with between 7 and 4 seconds left on the shot clock and 46.6 percent under four seconds left. Brunson bailing the Knicks out with tough shots late in possessions is usually a staple of their offense and something that demoralizes opposing defenses.

It's been part of a larger trend with the Knicks and their sluggish offense to start the year. As a team, they are shooting 30.4 percent from 7-to-4 seconds left in the shot clock and 26.5 percent under four seconds left. Those are the second-worst and worst marks in the NBA, respectively.

So often, as Brunson goes, the Knicks go. This is a clear example.

"He's taking the same shots as in the past," coach Mike Brown said Tuesday. "In my opinion, he's just missing shots. He's taking the right shots. I think all our guys are, for the most part, taking the right shots. Right now, they're not going in. And that can be for this reason, that reason, I don't know, and I'm not going to try to overanalyze it. As long as they keep taking the right shots, keep working on the shots, I think eventually they're gonna fall sooner than later."

Brown has coached some of the league's best-ever scorers, including LeBron James, Kobe Bryant and Stephen Curry. He has seen this before.

New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson (11) shoots a three-pointer against the Brooklyn Nets at Madison Square Garden in New York, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. Jason Szenes for NY Post

And he knows that usually, these ruts don't last too long.

"It happens," Brown said. "It happens to the best of them because everybody is definitely human and every human has their ups and their downs when it comes to shooting. That's why we have to keep embracing the little things, because they're not gonna always fall."

It's rare to see Brunson struggling the way he has to start this year.

But if he's taking the same shots as normal, it should be expected that the results will soon return to normal.

#2746. Poor situational football dooms Chiefs’ offense against Denver

The Kansas City Chiefs lost their second straight game, 28-24, against the Denver Broncos on Sunday, falling to 5-2. The loss propelled Denver to first place in the AFC West standings and should leave the Chiefs scratching their heads.

The Chiefs offense was fairly productive all game, with big plays from quarterback Patrick Mahomes and rookie running back Emmet Johnson.

Heading into the fourth quarter, the Chiefs led 24-13, but ended the game with a punt, a missed field goal, and a turnover on downs in the final minutes.

The Chiefs' offense outgained Denver by nearly 100 yards, but lingering third-down issues and poor situational football led to critical failures in the game's largest moments.

The fourth quarter started well for the Chiefs, with running back Kenneth Walker converting a third down and keeping the clock running.

After gaining four yards on a zone-read look on first down, Mahomes barely missed Kelce on second down on a pass that would have put the Chiefs past midfield and in the driver's seat.

On the ensuing third down, Mahomes would go to Johnson, who had a monster game up to that point.

This look is somewhere between an option and a rollout pass to Johnson. As it turned into a downfield pass, right tackle Jaylon Moore was deemed too far downfield, and officials called an illegal man downfield penalty; meanwhile, Johnson got as close as he could to a first down.

It is hard to know the series of events on the field, but Johnson was ruled down about a foot short of a first, and then Denver head coach Sean Payton declined the penalty, making it fourth-and-1.

No review of the play was made, but once Payton declined the penalty, this locked in his decision and would have given the Chiefs a chance to go for it on fourth down.

The Chiefs punt unit quickly ran to the field, where the ball was booted into the end zone for a touchback. Nine plays later, the Broncos scored and converted a two-point conversion to cut the deficit to three with less than nine minutes to play.

The Chiefs would start their next drive on a positive note as they looked to drive the ball and burn time off the clock.

With just under four minutes to play, the Chiefs had picked up another first down, with Walker and Johnson both contributing against a tired-looking Denver defensive front.

With the run game finally firing, and Denver on the ropes, the next set of Chiefs plays was baffling.

The Chiefs ran a screen to Rashee Rice outside, which, in theory, would strain the legs of the already-tired defense, but Rice made a poor choice to cut back inside instead of following his blocks to the outside and was tackled for only a two-yard gain.

On the next play, the Chiefs ran a similar look to Walker.

The screen to Walker appears to have been meant to take the defense by surprise, but they quickly swarm around Walker and prevent a larger gain. The play still gained six yards, and it would open up a manageable third-and-two.

The next play and ensuing decision would shape the end of the game.

The Chiefs' run game had been ineffective for most of the game, but Walker and Johnson had started to wear down the defense's tired legs.

The Chiefs came out of the gun needing two yards for a first, and they ran a rollout look, but the play quickly broke down. Walker is responsible for the first man off the line, but the edge rusher knocks him back, stopping the rollout. This disrupts Mahomes timing and prevents him from seeing Kelce flashing across the screen.

With no one else open, Mahomes takes a costly sack, putting the Chiefs in a situation where going for it on fourth and short is no longer an option.

Loyal Andy Reid trotted out Harrison Butker to attempt a 54-yard kick, and it ended up wide right.

The Broncos got the ball back in prime field position and scored in two plays to take a four-point lead.

The Chiefs got one more shot, and it came down to the red zone.

A monster Johnson kickoff return put the Chiefs in business, and it took them four plays to set up a first-and-goal at the Denver four-yard line. After an eight-yard shovel pass, the Chiefs let the clock run from 1:05 to 35 seconds.

A Walker run would move the ball to the one-yard line.

Out of timeouts, Denver could only wait, but then the Chiefs used a timeout of their own.

On their first crack from the one, the Chiefs went with an old favorite— the corndog —but Denver was ready.

With nine seconds to play, the Chiefs tried to run the ball again with Walker, but Denver was ready.

Denver's defensive line pinches down, and a free runner comes through at the line to stuff Walker for no gain.

On the next play, it appeared that the Chiefs had won, but a penalty on Moore wiped it away and set up a fourth-and-6.

On the game's final play, Mahomes would take a sack on a poorly designed look.

The play was poorly protected, and none of the Chiefs' receivers found any daylight againt the Broncos' man coverage.

There is more than one reason that led to this loss, but the poor situational football was a large culprit for the offenses implosion late in the game.

The Chiefs short yardage conversions have become an issue, and there is a path to succsuess, but it would involve the team doing something they have not done in over seven years.

The quarterback sneak is one of the most efficient plays in the history of the game, and the Chies blatant refusal to do so has cost the team due to a freak accident.

Even if the team decides to execute the plays with Mahomes on the sideline, backup quarterback Justin Fields should be more than capable of getting the job done.

The run game was bottled up, but the decsion to run a rollout look leading to a sack was inexcusable, especially when there was a hot hand like Johnson ready to go. Running the ball takes comitment, but if the rock is pounded enough times it will eventually break. Relying on one of the worst reciever rooms in the NFL to produce consistently in key moments is not an option.

The decsion to allow Butker kick, to only put the team up six points may be one of the worst of Reid's career.

The inability to score from the one yard line against a gassed defense with no timeouts, and relying on old tricks like "corndog" that half the field for a wizard like Mahomes can no longer be accpeted, especially when the main target runs out of bounds.

Starting one of the worst interor offensvie lienmen in the NFL inexplicably for the second time this season can also no longer be tolerated, especially when his body of work provides no evidence he has earned a stating spot, and his backup this week did not play with little context from the organization.

The 2026 Chiefs have the offensive talent to remain one of the leagues best units, and they showd what they are capable of multiple times through the course of the game. The key situations, and bad decisions on critical downs are what seperates them from a two game division lead, and the race they will be in with the Broncos the rest of the season.

The wrongs can me made right, but a plan needs to be put in place for these short yardage situations, what to do with Butker, and how the offensive line will look.

November is here, and as the schedule gets tougher, the games get bigger. It will be worth watching to see how the Chiefs perform as the pressure builds.

Oct 17, 2026; Waco, Texas, USA; TCU Horned Frogs quarterback Jaden Craig (1) looks to pass against the Baylor Bears during the second half at McLane Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

#2742. Avalanche sign star Cale Makar to largest contract in NHL history at $163.2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This has been the summer of spending in the NHL, and the Colorado Avalanche just broke the bank for star defenseman Cale Makar. On Friday, the team announced that Makar signed an eight-year extension worth $163.2 million.

The contract is the richest in league history -- both in total value and annual value at $20.4 million per year. Makar is the first player in NHL history to cross the $20 million salary threshold.

At 27-years old, Makar is arguably the best defensemen in the NHL, and he will remain in that conversation for quite a while. Makar has already won the Norris Trophy twice, and he was a key factor in Colorado's Stanley Cup run, which ended with him winning the Conn Smythe Trophy.

This past season, Makar posted monster numbers from the blue line yet again as he tallied 20 goals and 59 assists in 75 games. Since entering the NHL in 2019, Makar leads all defensemen in goals (20) and points (507).

"I am so excited and humbled to continue to wear the Avalanche sweater and represent this incredible organization and community," Makar said in a statement. "I would like to thank the Kroenke family, Joe Sakic and the entire Avalanche organization for their commitment, trust and belief in me. I would also like to thank my wife and family for their constant support, as well as Scott, Brian and Steve Bartlett for their guidance and assistance.

"To the Avalanche fans, thank you for your continued support and for welcoming us to Colorado years ago. Colorado has truly become a second home to us, and we are so grateful to be here. I look forward to getting back on the ice with my teammates and continuing to work toward our goal of bringing the Stanley Cup back to the Mile High City."

Over the last three seasons, Makar's impact has been immense in all three zones. He's posted a five-on-five expected goals share of 54.5%, per Natural Stat Trick. With Makar on the ice in those situations, Colorado has outscored its opponents 220-157. In two of the last three seasons, Makar has hit the 90-point mark, and he has 100-point potential at his best.

Makar's $11.4 million raise kicks in in at the start of the 2026-27 season, and it will make things significantly tighter for the Avalanche as they navigate the salary cap. The bright side for Colorado -- and the key in getting this deal done -- is that the team now has each of its core players signed through at least 2031.

There may be some sticker shock upon seeing the $20.4 million average annual value, but that's the new reality in the NHL as the cap rises exponentially. The previous record for highest salary in NHL history was just set earlier this offseason when the Anaheim Ducks signed center Leo Carlsson to a contract worth $18 million per year, and the Chicago Blackhawks announced a $75 million extension for Connor Bedard.

The next domino to fall will be an extension for Minnesota Wild defenseman Quinn Hughes, who is neck-and-neck with Makar as the best defensemen in the world. Waiting until after the Makar deal was announced to sign Hughes could prove to be a mistake for Wild general manager Bill Guerin.

#2739. One of Dave McGillivray's 7 marathons, 7 days event coming to Polar Park

That "run the bases" promotion is getting lapped. Instead of first to third, try first to 26th (point two).

The first-of-its kind New England 776 is coming to Polar Park in June as the baseball stadium adds another sport to its confines: distance running.

The event is a spinoff from the World Marathon Challenge, which is seven marathons, in seven days on seven continents. Boston Marathon race director Dave McGillivray completed the 7-7-7 in 2018 and has worked with colleagues Ron Kramer and Josh Milne to produce a local version, which includes the six New England states, with Massachusetts going to bat twice – and baseball stadiums will be frequent hosts.

The NE 776 begins on Sunday, June 6 at Hadlock Field in Portland, Maine – home of the Sea Dogs, Double-A affiliate of the Boston Red Sox. The next day, the event strides over to Polar Park. As in the marathon in Portland, runners will tread on the warning track to complete 26.2 miles.

Kramer, lead vehicle coordinator for the Boston Marathon since 1989, wheel-measured the Polar Park warning track and discovered that it will take 111.6 laps to equal a marathon.

A third ballpark with bat fifth in the lineup: Delta Dental Stadium in Manchester, N.H.

The idea of using baseball stadiums comes as no surprise for those who know McGillivray. After he ran from Medford, Oregon, to his hometown of Medford, Mass., over 80 days in 1978, McGillivray did a lap around the warning track at Fenway Park to put an exclamation point on his 3,452-mile feat.

McGillivray has also served as race director for the Fenway Park Marathon (116.1 laps), but ballparks actually weren't the first option for NE 776 sites.

"We were focused mainly on State Parks but came up with some scheduling challenges," he told the Telegram via email. "We even once considered all college campuses, but again scheduling was the challenge.

"(The ballparks) are very excited to host a marathon. Some venues wanted to host one of the races but couldn't do it on the only day we had available. In the end, it all still worked out great."

Other sites include the Ten Mile River Greenway (E. Providence, RI; marathon No. 3); Windsor Locks Canal State Park (Connecticut; marathon No. 4); Toonerville Rail Trail (Springfield, Vt.; marathon No. 6); and Hormel Stadium and Torbert Macdonald Park, the event's final marathon (Saturday, June 12) that ends at the Dave McGillivray Track in Medford.

McGillivray's other endurance feats include a 1980 East Coast Run (Winter Haven, Florida to Boston; 1,520 miles); eight Ironman triathlons; biking more than 1,000 miles through New England; and running 54 consecutive Boston Marathons.

The World Marathon Challenge ranks among his most difficult accomplishments.

"It was a thrill and I know lots of running friends who would like to do it themselves but the entry fee is out of their reach and just all the logistics can be daunting," McGillivray said. "So, I thought, why not do something similar right here at 'home'.  The response just in the past 24-hours since we announced it (Monday) has been incredible."

Runners have the choice of taking on all marathons or one of the seven. A 2- to 5-person relay team option is also available. A $1,000 fundraising commitment is required for each marathon. Money raised through the NE 776 will benefit the Dave McGillivray Finish Strong Foundation.

"Both the ultra (marathon) crowd and the non-ultra crowd can participate," McGillivray said. "There is something for everyone here."

Additional event and registration information is available at www.newengland776.com.

#2738. INTERVIEW: Philipp Lahm senses Harry Kane would trade Ballon d'Or for Champions League glory

MÜNCHEN (Bulinews) Former Bayern Munich star Philipp Lahm, speaking at a media round attended by Bulinews.com, was delighted with Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph but feels the striker would trade it in for top honours in Europe.

“It’s a personal award. I think [winning it] is more important for the offensive players rather than the rest. So, [someone like ex-Bayern star] Franck Ribery will be happy Kane won the Ballon d’Or.

“We all know how important the FC Bayern team is for Kane’s success too. Since I never had the chance to win this award, as a captain I think more of the team as a whole.

“I think Harry Kane would exchange his Ballon d’Or for a Champions League title. Most players grew up playing as a team from a very young age,” Lahm explained, alluding to the collective aspect of football teams.

Interestingly, the 2014 World Cup winner went on to explain why he feels it is difficult to win the Ballon d’Or as a German playing in the domestic top-flight. His theory is largely linked to external noise and catching the public eye.

“As for Kane and Michael Olise [ranked 9th in the Ballon d’Or], they came from another country. I think it’s quite difficult for a German player playing in the Bundesliga to win this award. Think of Florian Wirtz for example.

“It’s all about the attention. When you are successful with the German national team then you become visible. Then when you play successful football for a club like Liverpool, the attention in the UK is much bigger.

“That’s important for this award. It [less attention] makes it more difficult for a player to win it in the Bundesliga rather than changing to another league [and club]. But I do hope the best players stay in the Bundesliga.

“I hope with players like Harry Kane that a lot of other players will follow now it’s possible to win [the Ballon d’Or playing in the Bundesliga],” Lahm concluded, underlining his hope that others may be inspired by the Englishman.

#2737. 2026 NHL free agent tracker: Patrick Kane returns to Blackhawks on two-year contract

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NHL free agency has slowed down in late July, but some notable names are still coming off the board. Most notably, Patrick Kane is returning to the Chicago Blackhawks on a two-year contract worth $16 million, the team announced on Thursday.

Already a Chicago legend and future Hall of Famer, Kane won three Stanley Cups and a slew of individual awards with the franchise that selected him with the No. 1 overall pick in 2007. Kane's first stint with the Blackhawks lasted 16 seasons, and he piled up 446 goals and 779 assists in 1,161 games. Kane ranks inside the top five of just about every statistical category in franchise history, and he will get the chance to keep climbing those lists over the next two years.

The Blackhawks sent Kane to the New York Rangers at the 2023 NHL trade deadline, and he played just 19 regular season games there before hitting free agency the next summer. Hip surgery delayed Kane's decision until November of that year, but he ultimately landed with the Detroit Red Wings, where he's spent the last three seasons.

Last season was Kane's best with Detroit, and it proved that he still had some gas left in the tank, at least offensively. Kane posted 16 goals and 41 assists in 67 games -- with 19 of those points coming on the power play.

In his second stint with the Blackhawks, Kane will add another level of playmaking to the power play, and he should strengthen a top six forward group that's bereft of proven talent. Kane will also be an excellent mentor and sounding board for fellow No. 1 overall pick, Connor Bedard, who is set to miss the first month of the season after undergoing shoulder surgery.

Kane isn't the player he once was, but he'll give Chicago a bit more pop at the top of the lineup, and his first game back in a Blackhawks jersey will be a huge night for the city.

#2735. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#2734. Game Preview: Knicks vs. Bulls, November 4, 2026

One of the most dreaded speeches a head basketball coach has to make is the one where he talks up an obviously overmatched opponent. He knows the other squad will have plenty of trouble hanging with his ball club even on a good night. On a regular night, his troops would trash the opposition worse than the Globetrotters ever did the Washington Generals. Yet he also knows that complacency can ruin the best game plan and that arrogance has led many teams down the road to hell. Luckily for Mike Brown, he has recent history on his side for his pep talk about the Chicago Bulls.

Those very ballers nearly pulled off the upset against your world champions Knicks last week. Although it came on a second night of a back-to-back and in the not-so-friendly confines of the United Center, the warning should still resonate with the Bockers before they host one of the league's worst teams. Even if you could argue there isn't anybody worse than Thiago Splitter's young group so far this year.

Sitting at the bottom of the league at 1–6, the Bulls have already lost games by 19, 35, and 43 points and sport the worst point differential in the NBA. Yes, even the Sacramento Acuffs have Chicago beat in that regard. While the offense at times actually looks serviceable, the defense has been nothing short of abysmal. They allow 128.8 points per contest, and games against them regularly turn into a shootaround for the opposition. Defending downtown has been especially tough, with teams nailing almost 40 percent of their long-range shots against Chicago. Yes, they've faced some stiff competition, but come on.

People in the Windy City are fairly relaxed, though. With a new coach and a young star in the fold, 2026–27 was always going to be a rebuilding year, one they sorely needed after what felt like a decade of drowning in mediocrity. Caleb Wilson, the fourth overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, has been as good as advertised early on and finally gives Chicago fans something to look forward to. The former UNC highflyer is hardly efficient yet, makes plenty of rookie mistakes, and at times doesn't really know what this basketball thing is that he's doing out there. But man, does his game look promising.

Wilson is an ultra-modern combo forward with world-class athleticism and a good, determined head on his shoulders. He plays extremely hard, looks to be enjoying himself a ton out there, and seems to possess a drive you usually find only in the cream of the NBA's crop. If he adds a few pounds and works on his jumper, it's easy to see the 20-year-old becoming the centerpiece of whatever the Bulls envision for their future.

The same can't be said for Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis, also two promising young players who have struggled under new head coach Thiago Splitter. Giddey's scoring has dropped from 17 points per game last season to just nine this year, and he's shooting south of 37 percent from the field. Rumor has it a wrist injury is hampering the Australian, and it might be a problem all year.

Buzelis' excuse is that he's struggled out of the gate before. But even with a world of athletic talent and plenty of promise, he sometimes looks like one of those players who will never really put it all together. It's still way too early to give up on a 22-year-old as gifted as the former G League Ignite hooper. At some point, though, those gifts have to show up night in and night out on the NBA hardwood, well after the layup line.

Chicago's most accomplished veteran, Norman Powell, should help in that regard, but how much he can do is debatable. He probably hasn't even unpacked his suitcase yet, and he'll most likely be shipped out to a wannabe contender by the trade deadline. Is someone like that really going to change your culture? Powell has played very good ball for years, but can he be the guy who turns things around in Chicago? Your guess is as good as mine.

Even if Powell is exactly the vet presence Bulls ownership envisions, Splitter is still fighting an uphill battle. The roster is extremely young and short on inside brawn (sorry, Stix Smith, Zach Collins, and Nic "I can't lose to the Knicks" Claxton), reliable outside shooting, and any sort of cohesiveness. The losses should pile up pretty quickly. The Knicks should help their former rivals along and get back to .500 in this one. Anything else would be unacceptable.

But I'm sure Mike Brown will remind his team of that in his pregame speech.

Who: New York Knicks (3-4) vs Chicago Bulls (1-6)Date: Wednesday, November 4, 2026Time: 7:30 PM ETPlace: Madison Square Garden, NYCTV: MSGFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky
