#2733. Jets snap this NHL 9,652-game losing streak with latest 4-goal comeback in history

Jets snap this NHL 9,652-game losing streak with latest 4-goal comeback in history originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

A stellar start to the season for Canadiens rookie goaltender Jacob Fowler was derailed in unbelievable fashion on Tuesday night, with the Jets piecing together a rapid four-goal comeback in a matter of minutes.

Trailing 4-0 with under three minutes remaining, Winnipeg scored four times at the Bell Centre to force overtime, where momentum carried the Jets to a win.

It was the latest four-goal comeback in NHL history: before Tuesday, teams were 0-9,652-0 when trailing by at least four goals with less than three minutes remaining, ESPN's John Buccigross noted and 0-3,257 when scoreless in that scenario.

The comeback was an NHL first by some measures, leaving the Canadiens shell-shocked in front of their home crowd.

Here's a closer look at the Jets' historic comeback.

MORE:Ranking best and worst NHL 'Hometown Remix' jerseys

The Jets scored four goals in a span of two minutes and six seconds deep into the third period on Tuesday night, not scoring the first until there were only two minutes and 39 seconds on the clock in regulation.

Tyrel Bauer struck first, followed by a goal from Morgan Barron to cut the deficit to two. In the final minute of the period, Kyle Connor scored twice, 27 seconds apart, to stun the Canadiens and send the game to overtime.

Once the momentum starts shifting like that, it's hard to get it back. Montreal conceded the game-winning goal to Dylan Samberg three minutes and 30 seconds into overtime.

After the deflating loss, Canadiens star Cole Caufield said "guys thought the game was over."

"We had a four-goal lead," Caufield told reporters. "There's no excuse for this. It's terrible."

The Canadiens gave up 47 shots on goal in the win. Until the final three minutes, though, the rookie Fowler handled what came his way, as he has done throughout the early weeks of the season.

The start to the season has been much more challenging for the Jets -- they entered Tuesday fresh off a 7-0 loss to the Hurricanes -- but if there were ever a way to change the mood, a four-goal comeback is certainly on.

#2729. Lakers vs. Kings Preview: Quick road trip

After taking care of business at home, the Lakers (6-2) head to Sacramento where they will take on the Kings (1-6) for the first time this season. Both teams enter this matchup coming off wins.

Who: Los Angeles Lakers vs. Sacramento Kings

The Lakers responded to their worst loss of the young season by stringing together two straight victories, which wasn't an easy task considering that it happened in back-to-back games. Led by Luka Dončić, who is just scorching hot right now, Los Angeles stands at 6-2.

Simply put: if the Lakers continue to perform and win at this rate, there's little doubt they can secure a top-four spot in the Western Conference, health permitting. A big part of their success in finishing among the West's top four over the last couple of seasons has been their ability to take care of business against teams lower in the standings.

Enter the Kings, who have had a tough start to their season. Sacramento has won only one of their first seven games. They're 22nd in the league in points per game and are ranked 25th in offensive rating. The team is led by veterans Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis, but so far it's their rookie Darius Acuff Jr. who's stealing the limelight. Acuff Jr. is averaging 26.1 points per game, so he'll certainly be high on LA's scouting report.

That said, there's really no excuse for the Lakers to lose this game. They should be better in every facet and, while it's tougher to beat opponents on their home floor, Los Angeles' firepower should be enough to propel them to a win. Ideally, it's the type of victory that won't see Dončić play more than 36 minutes and that sees contributions across the board.

Maybe this is the perfect time for some of the role players to break out. Perhaps it's an opportunity for Quentin Grimes and Colin Sexton to regain his shooting rhythm or maybe a monster-like game for Walker Kessler, who held up very well against Giannis Antetokounmpo in the win against the Miami Heat.

Jake LaRavia — who has been playing really well to begin the season — should be able to continue making his presence felt while Sandro Mamukelashvili and Jarred Vanderbilt will be given the opportunity to do so. And how about a proper debut for rookie Cameron Carr? It would be nice to see him go up against Acuff Jr.

We'll see who comes up big for both teams as Pacific Division teams battle it out on Wednesday.

Aside from having the 25th best offensive rating in the league, the Kings also don't rebound the ball well (27th), just like the Lakers.

For the Lakers' injury report, only Adou Thiero (left knee injury management) is listed as out.

As for the Kings, Keegan Murray (left ankle capsulitis), Maxime Raynaud (right patella subluxation) and Ben Simmons (right achilles tendon repair) are out. Precious Achiuwa (left ankle soreness) is probable.

#2723. Opponent Breakdown: Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets Offense

Brent Key started last season 9-1 before losing three straight games to close out a strong season for a Georgia Tech program that hasn't had a lot of 9-win seasons as of late. Key faced lofty expectations this season after such a good season, but things have gone about as poorly as possible for Tech. The Yellow Jackets only have one FBS win this season, and they haven't been very competitive in most of their losses. Key will have to find a way to motivate his team as they enter the toughest stretch of their schedule.

The gamble of bringing in a backup quarterback to be your starter has worked well for Louisville. It has not gone well for Georgia Tech. Alberto Mendoza was the backup to his Heisman Trophy winning brother Fernando last season at Indiana. He entered the portal after the season, even though it would seem that he would be the next man up for the Hoosiers. That was not the case, as they went after the top quarterbacks in the portal and Brent Key made the choice to bring in Mendoza.

The Junior has been average with 10 touchdowns and 6 interceptions. He does have a high completion percentage this year at 70%, but his 222 yards per game leaves a lot to be desired. Mendoza also has 7 fumbles this year, with a lot of them coming from poor ball handling in the pocket. There have been some good moments as he has looked good throwing the ball down the field, as well as scrambling to avoid pressure. But overall, he has not done enough to unlock the potential of this offense.

Running back is a position that had high hopes going into this season with the addition of Justice Haynes from Michigan. Haynes has been solid with 78 yards rushing per game, but it is a lot of tough yardage for him. He is averaging 4.9 yards per carry as there has not been a lot of room for him to run. Haynes has the talent to be a problem for an inconsistent Louisville run defense, as he runs very hard and can break a long run if he gets into the open field.

Trelain Maddox leads the Yellow Jackets in touchdown runs this season as the change of pace back for this team. Maddox has good speed in the open field while also showing the ability to make people miss. Maddox and Malachi Hosely could be factors in this game if they are both healthy. Tech will look to sustain drives to keep Louisville's offense on the sidelines. That will take a good effort from these running backs.

Former Louisville commit, Jordan Allen as emerged as the top receiver for Tech this year. The speedy sophomore has shown that he has genuine playmaking ability as a slot receiver as well as a returner. Allen has 46 catches on the season, but his lack of explosive plays are part of the reason the offense is struggling. Allen has one touchdown this year, and his longest catch is for 46 yards. What is really shocking to me is that they have not used him on jet sweeps or other handoffs. He only has one carry this year.

Dalen Penson and Kevin Roche are the other top targets for this Tech offense. Pinson is an outside receiver who is the most likely player to be utilized for deep shots down the field. However, he can make plays at all three levels of the offense and the offense does a good job of finding situations where he wins. Roche is a 6-9 tight end who is always open. Mendoza has done a good job of putting the ball in spots where Roche can use his height. He is not the fastest player, but he can run well enough to get open down the field. Look for him to be the top option in the red zone.

Key's teams have been known for their very good offensive lines, but losing Geep Wade as the position coach appears to be a very big deal for this team. The Tech offensive line is among the worst in the country per PFF, and they don't pass the eye test either. Pass rushers have had a field day getting home with any sort of pressure approach. Mendoza has not helped himself, but if your line can't handle any blitz, you are not going to have a lot of time to throw the ball. Throw in their inability to open up rushing lanes for the backs, and this line has been a true letdown for this offense.

#2722. The Celtics need more from Derrick White and Payton Pritchard

Over the past few years, the Celtics have seen a lot of guards come and go. Marcus Smart, Malcolm Brogdon, Jrue Holiday and Anfernee Simons have all come in and eventually been shipped out.

In that timespan, both Derrick White and Payton Pritchard have remained in green. Pritchard, a 2020 draft pick, and White, acquired at the 2022 trade deadline, have been the guards Boston has chosen to lead them going forward.

However, to start this season, neither of them are playing very well.

Neither White nor Pritchard have gotten off to the starts Boston was looking for. White has averaged 11.1 points and 4.9 assists, shooting 44% from the field and 32% from three while Pritchard has averaged 13.4 points and 3.4 assists, shooting 40% from the field and 31% from three.

Unfortunately, Boston doesn't have a ton of depth at the point guard spot. Baylor Scheierman is much more of a 2-guard or a wing than a point guard and Mike Conley is 40-years-old.

CLEVELAND, OHIO – OCTOBER 08: Devin Carter #99 celebrates with Mike Conley #45 of the Boston Celtics during the first quarter of a preseason game against the Cleveland Cavaliers at Rocket Arena on October 08, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. The Celtics defeated the Cavaliers 124-113. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Devin Carter is another option, but he has yet to play this season due to mononucleosis and could have a role when he returns. With that said, he is a two-way guard who hasn't had a good start to his NBA career so we shouldn't be putting too much stock in him.

Boston needs the improved play to come from White and Pritchard. Those are the guys they have invested in.

For Pritchard, he needs to be more aggressive. Joe Mazzulla should be starting him, but that is a different conversation. Regardless, the Celtics need Payton to be a big scorer for them, in whatever role he is in. So far this season, Pritchard is averaging 10.3 shots per game, below both his 2024-25 and 2025-26 averages. If you remove the two games against the Bulls, Pritchard is averaging 7.8 shots per game, along with just 7.2 points.

That cannot happen on this team. In an ideal world, Pritchard is the Celtics number 2 offensive option behind Jayson Tatum, to take pressure off of White and Paul George. He isn't going to be that without being aggressive.

Derrick White has always been more of a defensive player than offensive player, and so far this season, the Celtics have been a worse defensive team with him out there. According to databallr, Boston is 4.8 points better in 131 minutes with White on the bench than they are in the 210 minutes White has been on the court. It's a small sample size, but I'm not too concerned.

I am worried about is his three-point shot though. Since the start of last season, D-White's three-point shot has fallen off of a cliff. In the three seasons prior to last year, he shot 39% from three in the regular season. Since the start of last season, White has shot 33% from beyond the arc. He needs to make more threes than he has over the past year plus.

White and Pritchard are too talented and too good to play this poorly all season. Water typically finds its level with this stuff and I expect it to do the same here. If they don't start playing better, however, it will be very hard for the Celtics to accomplish anything real in April and May.

#2720. Lions scouting report: Dolphins’ strengths, weaknesses

After back-to-back stressful divisional victories at home, the Detroit Lions get a bit of a break and head down to Florida to take on the Miami Dolphins. Detroit is on a three-game winning streak, and we've seen the defense take a step in the right direction to complement this offense. The Lions are finding their groove, it seems, and taking on a struggling team could be big for them.

Miami is coming off another loss and aiming higher and higher at getting the top pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. The team hasn't been strong on either side of the ball; the offense is missing playmakers because of injuries or skill set, and while the defense has talent, it hasn't had enough impact on the field.

Let's take a deep look at the Dolphins' season so far as they head into Week 9.

Week 1: Lost to Las Vegas Raiders 27-13Week 2: Lost to San Francisco 49ers 35-13Week 3: Lost to Kansas City Chiefs 24-10Week 4: Lost to Minnesota Vikings 15-10Week 5: Lost to Cincinnati Bengals 31-24Week 6: BYEWeek 7: Defeated New York Jets 28-25Week 8: Lost to New England Patriots 24-19

The offense has been the roughest part of the Dolphins team this season. Newly signed quarterback Malik Willis was given the keys to the starting job, but the supporting cast isn't the same as it was in Green Bay. He's thrown for six touchdowns, five interceptions, and is averaging 181.1 yards per game. His legs have helped a lot, as he's averaging 6.3 yards per carry, amassing 225 yards, and three touchdowns.

When he isn't running the ball, second-year running back Ollie Gordon is. Gordon took over for De'Von Achane after Achane tore his ACL in Week 3, ending his season. Gordon is averaging 4.5 yards per carry, with 408 yards and a team-high four rushing touchdowns, sparking an offense that desperately needs help.

Willis has struggled to pass as well; his top wide receiver, Malik Washington, has 31 catches for 329 yards, and tight end Greg Dulcich has 22 catches for 256 yards. Receivers Caleb Douglas and Kevin Coleman have found the end zone most often among the group, combining for four touchdowns (two each) with 21 catches for 308 yards.

Willis' offensive line has also struggled to give him time to throw. According to PFF, the line has the second-lowest pass-blocking grade (53.6). Willis has been sacked 21 times this season, the seventh-highest in the NFL. Run blocking is better, but not by much, ranking 27th with a 55.9 grade. Miami has had to rely on the ground game to stay alive, as Willis just doesn't have the time or the weapons in the passing attack to make teams nervous.

On defense, there isn't much to say on the positive side. While they aren't the worst in the league, they're near the lower end in a few areas. The Dolphins are tied for the fewest sacks in the NFL with nine, led by EDGE Chop Robinson's four.

The secondary has been struggling as well, with rookie safety Michael Taaffe leading the team with two interceptions. The Dolphins have allowed the highest completion percentage in the NFL (76.9 percent) and are tied for second-most 40+ yard passing plays with eight, according to Next Gen Stats. Once again, a safety leads the way in pass deflections with three by Dante Trader, as this unit can't seem to get their hands on the ball often.

While the secondary is struggling to make plays, the run defense hasn't been up to par for the Dolphins either, ranked 31st by PFF with a grade of 51. They've allowed only three rushing plays of over 20 yards, the longest being 27, but could still improve by slowing down opposing offenses on the ground. Miami is ranked 26th in tackling with a grade of 48.2 and has 47 missed tackles this season, the eighth most in the league, per PFF.

Key players ruled out: RB De'Von Achane (IR)Key players to monitor: G/T Kadyn Proctor (concussion)

When it comes to injuries, the Dolphins' only major star who's injured is Achane. Luckily for Miami, they have some good depth at the position. Rookie offensive lineman Kadyn Proctor is in concussion protocol, as he's the only other key player currently dealing with a notable injury.

When Achane went down, it looked like this struggling offense was about to take a giant step back. Not so fast, my friend, as Gordon would say. He's helped give the ground game some life. While Achane never found the end zone this season, Gordon surged ahead of Willis in rushing touchdowns in his three starts. He's become another solid running back for this team, and when Achane returns in 2027, this duo will be another stellar one-two punch.

Miami doesn't have weapons in the passing game, and Willis is the only strength there. Willis also likes to run the ball, but he can't do it all, and having Gordon with him gives this offense a better chance for success. If the running game struggles, this offense will collapse. For now, though, they are what is keeping them in these games offensively.

While the offense has started to figure some things out over the past three weeks, the defense is still struggling. It doesn't matter if it's on the ground or through the air; teams are having their way. Is it the worst defense in the NFL? No, but it's in the bottom tier, and there aren't many signs it's heading in the right direction. They have created six turnovers this season, tied for the third-fewest in the NFL according to ESPN.

Their run defense is a step above their passing defense, but against the Lions this week, that secondary will need to play the best game of their lives. Detroit's offense will be one of the best offenses they've faced this year. They put up a fight with the Cincinnati Bengals and the Kansas City Chiefs, so the effort is there, but it will need to be better than those two matchups.

The defense has very few playmakers on their side of the ball too, as Robinson is arguably one of the best players on this team. Former first-round pick defensive tackle Kenneth Grant hasn't lived up to the hype, and the team can't afford its top-end players to flail out. The best way this defense can improve is by forcing turnovers and keeping the field short so the offense has a better chance to put up points.

Key matchup: Lions run defense vs. Dolphins run offense

I'm not worried about this Lions offense putting up points against this Dolphins' lackluster defense. The Lions defense has been inconsistent this season, especially against the run. While the secondary has garnered a lot of attention, rightfully so, the run defense hasn't been quite up to the standard the team likes to be at. The Dolphins' passing attack doesn't scare me, even with the Lions' secondary being their weakest link.

Detroit lost a few players who can help stop the run against the Vikings—linebacker Jack Campbell is a big help in run defense, and fellow linebacker Jimmy Rolder was put in IR—leaving potential holes at the position. Co-sack leader D.J. Wonnum and safety Brian Branch left the game with concussions after they collided. While Branch helps the secondary, he does a solid job filling run fits to limit what running backs do at the next level.

If Miami can run the ball well against Detroit, this game could be closer than people anticipate. This isn't just about stopping Gordon; it's also about containing Willis so he doesn't damage you with his running ability. The Lions have faced off against quarterbacks who can use their legs, like Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen, for the most damage, with 69 rushing yards. Willis will probably be their next toughest challenge with his feet, so the front seven need to contain him and keep him inside the pocket so he can't escape.

Vegas line for Sunday: Lions favored by 7

#2718. The Celtics are showing progress attacking the rim, but there’s room to grow

In his season-ending press conference immediately after Boston's first-round playoff exit, Brad Stevens made a comment about the state of the Celtics that reverberated through every offseason decision leading up to the start of the season.

"I think one of the things that we've gotta figure out is how to have more impact at the rim," Stevens said. "I thought we struggled to get to where we wanted to go on offense."

He had a point. In the regular season, the Celtics were dead last in volume inside of 5 feet, averaging 22 attempts per game. But on low volume came high efficiency, with the team's 69% finishing on those attempts being second in the league. On top of that lack of attempts was a league-low in free throw attempts (18.7).

So, the Celtics made changes. They brought in Mitchell Robinson, one of the game's best offensive rebounders after the Celtics averaged the lowest amount of putback points among all playoff teams (4.1). Then they swapped Paul George for Jaylen Brown, adding a shot creator that would offer a different kind of off-ball influence to open up Jayson Tatum's own scoring creation.

As of Nov. 2, Boston's 7-game starting sample has shown early returns in this area. As far as just touching the paint, they're getting inside at an increased rate, jumping from 24.4 touches to 28.3. The Celtics entered their Rockets matchup 13th in field goal attempts inside of 5 feet, making a major leap of 28.3 attempts to last year's 22.

There's work to be done in their finishing on those attempts — they're currently working at a 63% clip (17th in the league) — but the results are showing a team that's making an effort to get more looks at close range.

This back-to-back showed two sides of that progress, with slight variations in personnel and significant variations in Joe Mazzulla's lineups.

On the first night of their back-to-back, the Celtics got an Orlando team that's missing key pieces and is in the process of developing a new identity under coach Sean Sweeney, yet still retains some of that gritty defensive identity with their available personnel.

For Boston, only Mitchell Robinson was absent from the rotation, and in that absence, we saw more of the freeflowing, fast-reacting movement of last year's offense with Neemias Queta as the lone big on the floor.

It's no surprise that Robinson and Queta lead the team in paint touches, but behind them stand Boston's two most important players in Tatum (3.5) and George (3). In this matchup, they shined both in their self-creation and in their playmaking inside the paint.

As a team Boston was 72% inside the restricted area, and Tatum's gravity as a pick-and-roll ballhandler was a significant factor in creating looks for himself and for the roller.

Tatum's high free throw rate has also been a major benefit of his driving aggression. The Celtics are currently averaging 28 attempts from the line, another significant jump from last year's number. Tatum is currently at 10.2 attempts from the line.

Like Tatum, George is creating off the dribble, feeding the roll man, and comfortably playing off-ball.

It's two players who have figured out how to put the ball into space. But for that to happen, you need good cutting instincts from those around them. That wasn't an issue last year, and it's definitely not an issue now. The Celtics are currently scoring 1.35 points per cut possession, nearly identical to last year's 1.36 PPP.

This game was a good indicator of this team's ceiling attacking the rim. You're missing Robinson, who has struggled to adapt to his new role closer to the action on the perimeter, but you're seeing Boston's other two bigs look comfortable in their roles, while the team's two stars acted as high-running motors to an efficient offense. When you can space the floor with shooters around Tatum and George and add in a rolling threat like Queta, the space to attack and the decisions you can make feel more abundant.

On the second night of their back-to-back, the Celtics were without their other primary offseason addition with Paul George getting a night off.

On a sluggish shooting night, the primary theme for this story's subject was as follows: No Tatum=No Paint Pressure.

Without George's primary option lineup, when Tatum stepped off the floor, getting inside the arc became a chore for Boston. In a shade under 16 minutes with Tatum resting, they were just 1-for-8 on shots inside the paint, with a single shot generated at the rim. With Tatum, they had 20 shots at the rim and were 70% on those shots, much more in line with what we've seen so far this season.

Along with his ability to create in isolation, Tatum's gravity as a pick-and-roll threat opened up rim-runs for Mitchell Robinson and Queta, while his vision finding cutters particularly flashed early on.

The Celtics trailed by five when Tatum checked out with 1:39 left in the third quarter. When he returned with 7:02 left to go in the fourth quarter, it was a deficit of 16. With JT off the floor in general, the Celtics were outscored 35-18.

When he returned, it didn't take long for the offense to get back into its previous flow. Tatum quickly assisted on a drive-and-kick three to Derrick White in the corner, hit Queta on a roll, and scored himself on a drive-and-finish within his first six possessions after checking back in. But by then, the Rockets had comfortably separated enough to bury them.

With a lack of paint pressure coming from the perimeter, Mazzulla experimented heavily with double-big rotations throughout the game, which in spurts gave Boston some more putback and lob options but wasn't nearly enough to overcome poor shooting from the outside and a tough night on drives. The Queta-Robinson combo was featured most prominently, finishing the night with 4:42 on the floor together. With those two sharing the floor, the Celtics were 3-for-3 at the rim, two of which came from Queta and the other from Robinson.

Even without an interior enforcer like Steven Adams, the Rockets are an exceptionally difficult team to get a step on. They have a collection of lengthy wing defenders like Amen Thompson, Tari Eason and Kevin Durant and feisty point-of-attack guards in Marcus Smart, Fred VanVleet and Reed Sheppard. Add to that disciplined help on the nail, and even if your last line of defense is Alperen Sengun, the defense is designed to make it drudgerous just to get to that weak link. And it just so happens that their weak link still finished with a pair of blocks and steals on Monday night.

If the Orlando game was a sign of what they could be, Houston was a sign of how far they have to go to get there. Missing George's ballhandling was a predictable blow, but a lack of influence in the paint from those not named Jayson Tatum against a quality defense does show that they have a lot to work on.

The road ahead is long to figure out what kind of impact this team can have from close range. They can't all be against a Chicago, and they won't all be against a Houston or Detroit, but it's important that every step of the way, we keep tabs on the progress of this team's still-developing interior identity.

#2716. Week 8, 3 down and 3 down: No silver lining from the Monsoon Bowl

The Atlanta Falcons played the role of Artax from The Neverending Story, and like Atreyu, Falcons fans' cries and pleas went unanswered as they watched their team slowly drown in the swamp. There is no up this week; everyone sank in the pit. Here's the Week 8, 3 down and 3 down.

This is what the worst version of Penix looks like. The slow starts have been there all season, but the turnovers have not. He's a rhythm passer, but that's a two-way street; once he gets off beat, he stays there. When he finds his groove, he is one of the more efficient passers out there.

Yes, the game plan was poor and so was the weather, but that doesn't mean you carelessly throw off your back foot, or throw into double/triple coverage. Everyone has bad games; I don't expect Penix to look this bad again, but it's up to him to make sure that doesn't happen.

The guard received his extension based on his potential, and he isn't living up to it. Unlike others on the line, he isn't a lineman with a typical outside-zone build; he has the physical traits that should transfer to a gap or duo scheme, but the team hasn't had much success running these concepts behind him.

Of all the Falcons linemen, he is the one who doesn't get to use the size excuse many have applied to the Buccaneers-Falcons mismatch, but he was routinely manhandled. If Bergeron can't turn things around, he'll be the first black eye on Cunningham's resume, because no matter how this season goes, they are tied to him through the 2027 season.

The Falcons didn't allow a single reception in this game, but they did allow 324 rushing yards. The rookie linebackers struggled all game, and the attacking scheme's aggressive nature is being taken advantage of by gap schemes, and Jeff Ulbrich is out of answers. He's increased the number of defensive line slants, a technique that essentially has his defenders line up in one gap and shoot into another, but it doesn't really solve the problem.

For starters, it's a guessing game; the defense doesn't know where the ball is going and is hoping to catch the offense off guard, but they aren't. The other issue is that against a gap scheme, they block down most of the time, so even if you move into a new gap, the OL isn't necessarily unprepared; they just need to play sound and pick up whoever shows up. Injuries to the front have definitely taken their toll on the defense, so the struggles are understandable. It is also worth noting that 229 of those 324 yards came after contact, and the weather definitely played a role in that statistic.

Something's gotta give. If you want to be treated like a winning team, you have to perform against good opponents, and the Falcons run game has been stuffed in a locker for four straight weeks. The reality is, they're just not that good, and Bijan can't cover up their poor blocking every week. Tommy Rees' lack of confidence showed immediately in his decision to come out throwing in a monsoon. He isn't putting forth a good enough effort to throw the run game away so early.

After their best week with multiple tight end personnel groups, the young coordinator tried to do everything out of 11 personnel (3 WRs, 1 TE), which let Tampa Bay stay in nickel all game. He did implement more pulling concepts this week but did far less gap and inside zone. It feels like the team is just aimlessly throwing things at the wall and hoping it sticks, but nothing is.

I highlighted Watts last week as someone who's had an underwhelming second year, but I also pointed out that I was nitpicking a bit as he hasn't truly been "bad." That is not the case this week; Watts was awful. Just like Penix, that was his worst performance as a Falcon. His run fits were nightmarish, constantly misreading leverage and putting himself out of position.

The open-field tackling was brutal and spurred many of the explosive runs. The young safety will get a lot more chances to play the pass next week, and let's hope that helps him get some confidence back.

Folk is cooked, washed, etc. The 41-year-old team captain will unfortunately not be the solution to the Falcons multi-year kicking struggles. Hard to use weather as an excuse when Chase McLaughlin posts a perfect day. The Falcons have no confidence in the kicker beyond 50, and we're starting to see them not have any within 50. Folk signed a 2-year deal, but Atlanta can cut him without any financial drawbacks at the end of the season; back to the drawing board.

It'll take a while to get the mud out of those new red jerseys. The Falcons probably won't play in a monsoon again this year, but that doesn't mean there wasn't plenty to learn from this outcome. Their process coming in was flawed, and they've now dropped to third place. Things won't get easier as they are set to face the explosive Bengals offense in Spain.

#2715. Has any country hosted a Cricket World Cup without qualifying? How Namibia can co-host 2027 ODI WC and still fail to qualify

Has any country hosted a Cricket World Cup without qualifying? How Namibia can co-host 2027 ODI WC and still fail to qualify originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Namibia has failed to qualify directly for the 2027 World Cup Qualifier despite co-hosting the tournament.

They must now come through an eight-team playoff in Nepal from December 4 to 21.

Ireland and the Netherlands hosted matches at the 1999 World Cup without qualifying for it.

Namibia will co-host the 2027 ODI World Cup alongside South Africa and Zimbabwe, with six matches scheduled at the Namibia Cricket Ground in Windhoek. They are now three tournaments away from playing in it.

Namibia finished outside the top four of the CWC League 2, which means they have missed direct entry to the World Cup Qualifier and must instead enter the Qualifier Play-off in Nepal.

South Africa and Zimbabwe, as Full Members, received automatic places as hosts. Namibia, an Associate, did not receive an automatic place, and the ICC pathway now requires them to win in Kathmandu, then in the Qualifier, and potentially a third time on their own ground in Windhoek.

MORE: Sandpapergate at Cape Town, South Africa: Revisiting the ball-tampering scandal that rocked Australian cricket eight years on

The first stage is the CWC Qualifier Play-off in Nepal from December 4 to 21, 2026. Eight teams compete, with hosts Nepal joined by Namibia, Canada, the UAE, Jersey, Kuwait, Italy, and Uganda. Only the top four advance.

Those four then join the West Indies, Ireland, the USA, Scotland, the Netherlands, and Oman at the CWC Qualifier, staged across South Africa and Namibia from February 26 to March 11, 2027. Namibia could therefore host the tournament that decides their fate.

Winning that Qualifier outright earns a place in Group A at the World Cup alongside India, Australia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Zimbabwe. Second, third, and fourth place sends a team to the Super Series instead.

The Super Series is a three-team round robin in Namibia on October 2, 4, and 6, 2027, with only the top side progressing to Group B, where England, South Africa, New Zealand, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh are waiting. The other two are eliminated.

That is the full picture. Finish top four in Nepal, win the Qualifier, and Namibia is in Group A. Finish second, third, or fourth in the Qualifier, and they must win a three-team tournament at home in Windhoek in the opening week of the World Cup itself to reach Group B.

MORE: ICC Cricket World Cup 2027 full schedule: Complete fixtures, dates, venues, match timings, and key details

Yes, and the precedent is recent enough to matter. The 1999 ODI World Cup was staged across England, Wales, Scotland, Ireland, and the Netherlands, with Ireland and the Netherlands each hosting a match despite failing to come through qualifying.

Only England received direct entry. Scotland, Ireland, and the Netherlands all had to take the qualification route as non-Full Members, and Scotland alone made it, becoming the first Associate nation to play a World Cup match on home soil.

Kenya in 2003 was a different case. They co-hosted alongside South Africa and Zimbabwe and qualified automatically because they held full ODI status, then reached the semi-finals, still the only non-Test nation to do so at a men's ODI World Cup.

The T20 World Cup has produced one comparable example. The 2021 edition was officially hosted by India but played in the UAE and Oman, and while Oman came through the qualifiers, the UAE did not. In 2024, the United States and West Indies both received automatic places as co-hosts.

England, with matches in Wales, Scotland, Ireland, and the Netherlands

England (direct qualification) and Scotland played. Ireland and the Netherlands did not qualify.

South Africa and Zimbabwe qualified automatically as Full Member hosts. Namibia must come through the Qualifier Play-off in Nepal.

India (official host), played in the UAE and Oman

India and Oman played. The UAE did not qualify.

No. Every named host has played in all 13 women's ODI World Cups from 1973 to 2025, and the same is true of the 10 women's T20 World Cups to 2026. Hosting has always gone to established Full Members such as England, India, New Zealand, Australia, South Africa, the West Indies, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh.

Since Paolo Banchero (ankle) and Jalen Suggs (knee) have been out, Orlando has been unable to find consistent offense and turnovers (17.3 per game; tied for 25th) are a massive issue.

No team is allowing more 3-pointers per game (17.3). The defense has been a nightmare, with players even saying they're not trusting each other on the court.

They've lost four consecutive and the warning sign is an offense that has is drastically underperforming; Charlotte ranks dead last in offensive rating (100.4), which is nearly four full points below the next closest team.

Are the Wizards finally a player in the East? The early returns on this group look good, but the schedule hasn't exactly been a slog.

They look older and slower, but the more curious issue is the sweeping dip across Nikola Jokić's stats: 22.0 points, 9.7 rebounds and 9.0 assists per game.

They've won three of four, but became the first team to lose to the previously winless Kings. The Cooper Flagg-Kyrie Irving partnership, however, has been a fun watch.

They've had five different leading scorers through eight games and lead the NBA in assists per game (30.6) and assist-to-turnover ratio (2.08). The results have nonetheless been uneven.

Are we in championship hangover territory? The Knicks are a bit of a rarity, ranking dead last in pace (96.5). They've struggled against marquee opponents.

No team has been hauling in more offensive boards per game (15.3), but losses in three of their last five have stunted their progress up the standings. And they got good news: Kawhi Leonard (knee swelling) might be back soon.

They share the ball well and protect it, but the Cavs have had an uneven start to the season. A loss against an extremely short-handed Thunder team was a missed opportunity.

They've won five consecutive, some against top-level teams (Lakers, Timberwolves, Nuggets). And Stephen Curry, at 38 years old, is playing his way into the MVP conversation.

Minnesota's two victories this week were against the Clippers and the Bucks, which is fine. But the Timberwolves will need to show that they can beat some of the league's better teams without Anthony Edwards. The saving grace will be the defense.

The overtime loss against the Pelicans was a setback, but Memphis remains the biggest surprise in the NBA, and Ty Jerome (28.2 points per game; seventh in the NBA) has been a revelation.

Losing Ja Morant (hamstring) is certainly a blow, but Portland has been doing a great job on the glass, limiting teams to an 10.0 second chance points per game.

The move to add Mitchell Robinson is paying off so far, as pairing him alongside Neemias Queta has Boston ranking third in the league in opponent points in the paint per game (39.4).

Recent competition hasn't been as robust, but the Spurs have won five consecutive and are taking care of the ball, ranking second in turnovers per game (13.4).

Luka Dončić is flaming opponents, averaging an absurd 38.3 points per game and orchestrating the NBA's best offense (121.9 points per 100 possessions).

They've dropped two of their last three, as the injuries keep piling up. The latest, to Chet Holmgren, means OKC will be without three starters for the foreseeable future.

It's rather unfair to drop a team one spot even though it won all three games this week. This is more about how good the 76ers have been and the quality of opponents Detroit faced. But can the Pistons sustain this level with Duncan Robinson (a career-high 17.9 points per game) as their second-leading scorer?

Interestingly, it's the defense that has been Philly's strength. The Sixers have the league's third-best defensive rating (105.1 points allowed per 100 possessions).

They own the NBA's top net rating (+12.8), Alperen Şengün is anchoring the offense and Jabari Smith Jr. is breaking out.

#2713. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2712. These 3 teams will miss the College Football Playoff despite being in 12-team bracket now

These 3 teams will miss the College Football Playoff despite being in 12-team bracket now originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Will the third time be the charm for BYU?

For the third straight season, the Cougars opened in the top 12 of the College Football Playoff rankings when the first set was unveiled Tuesday night.

That's a good omen 75% of the time the last two years. Nine of the top 12 teams inside the bracket after the first ranking made the College Football Playoff in each of the last two seasons.

That means three teams have missed each of those years.

BYU, of course, has fallen out both times. The Cougars were No. 7 in the first rankings last season but did not make the CFP. Notre Dame (No. 10) and Texas (No. 11) also missed the playoff. In 2024, Miami (No. 4), BYU (No. 9) and Alabama (No. 11) missed the playoff.

With that in mind, which three teams inside the top 12 will miss the College Football Playoff this year? Here are our three best bets.

BENDER: Winners (SEC) and losers (Notre Dame) from first CFP ranking

We hate doing this to Kentucky because the Wildcats have been one of the best stories in the SEC this season under first-year coach Will Stein. But the fact the Wildcats are already behind two-loss Alabama shows the committee doesn't really believe yet, and that 45-17 head-to-head loss to the Crimson Tide on Sept. 12 could resurface later.

That does not make it right. Alabama is the most overvalued team in the first rankings, and the Crimson Tide could take a third loss at No. 14 LSU in Week 10. But the committee is setting a precedent that hurts Kentucky if the team cannot take care of business in November.

The Wildcats have one of the toughest remaining schedules among the contenders. No. 13 Tennessee, No. 24 Florida and No. 18 Missouri complete the SEC schedule, and all that precedes a rivalry game against Louisville. Those teams have a combined record of 22-10.

Kentucky will have to go 3-1 in that stretch. Otherwise, they will get lost in the three-loss shuffle among the SEC playoff hopefuls, even with the 35-34 overtime victory against LSU on Oct. 10.

MORE: What a 24-team bracket would look like

BYU could win 10 games for the third straight season and still not make the College Football Playoff. This projection changes if the Cougars win the much-anticipated "Holy War" against No. 3 Utah. That would give BYU a cleaner look at a second straight Big 12 championship game appearance and a first CFP playoff berth.

A loss to the Utes, who are 4.5-point favorites, complicates that path. No. 15 Texas Tech does not play BYU or Utah, and the Red Raiders have one conference loss. BYU's 39-31 overtime loss at UCF hurts just as much as the 28-24 victory against No. 11 Notre Dame helps. The Big 12 is unlikely to get three playoff teams – especially seeing how the committee treated one-loss Texas Tech.

BYU cannot make the CFP without at least getting to the Big 12 championship game, and that is why it has to beat the Utes. BYU has won the last three meetings by a combined total of 13 points. If Notre Dame beats Miami and Utah beats BYU – and that is our prediction – the Cougars are in trouble.

MORE: Picks against the spread for epic Week 10 slate

The Rebels are the third-highest ranked two-loss team among the SEC crowd, and it might be too difficult to leap ahead of Alabama, who is five spots higher, and Texas, who beat the Rebels 34-27 on Oct. 24.

There remains a lot to like about Ole Miss, starting with quarterback Trinidad Chambliss, who leads the SEC with 2,189 passing yards. The Rebels average 37.1 points per game. This assessment changes dramatically if Ole Miss beats No. 2 Georgia on Saturday. This is the de facto elimination game for the Rebels.

A third loss would push the Rebels behind No. 11 Notre Dame and No. 12 Ohio State, teams that probably should be ranked ahead of them now. Plus, that 52-28 loss at Florida on Sept. 26 remains an eye-sore.

Ole Miss does have a 32-24 victory on LSU on its resume, but that is the only win against a team that is currently ranked in the CFP Top 25.

#2709. Patrick Dumont purchases Miriam Adelson’s share of Mavericks, now owns 69% of team

In 2023, Mark Cuban sold what was then his majority stake in the Dallas Mavericks to Miriam Adelson and her son-in-law, Patrick Dumont. At the time, the sale was purported to be to the tune of $3.5 billion. The transaction gave Adelson and Dumont majority ownership of the franchise, with Dumont serving in the role of Governor while Cuban maintained a minority stake in the team.

It is now being reported that another sale took place last month, though this one does not involve any new parties entering the fold. Adelson has instead sold her stake in the Mavericks to Dumont and his wife (and Adelson's daughter) Sivan Ochshorn. As a result of the deal, Dumont now holds a 69% ownership stake.

Along with Dumont are minority owners Cuban (27%) and Mary Stanton (4%). As part of the terms of the original sale in 2023, Dumont retains the right to purchase as much as 20% of Cuban's remaining portion as well. "Our plan is to look at that and to do that over time," Dumont suggests. Should he chose to do so, he would then hold a whopping 89% of the franchise which Forbes values at $5.8 billion.

Since taking over in 2023, Dumont has overhauled much of the front office. He hired Rick Welts as CEO, Ethan Casson as President (and successor CEO come the turn of the calendar to 2027), Masai Ujiri, Mike Schmitz, new head coach Dusty May and a number of other senior-manager level employees. Dumont is also hard at work on a new basketball-only area for the Mavs, with plans to make the former Valley View Mall an all-out entertainment destination.

"The most important thing every day is just trying to work harder to get better." Dumont clearly has big plans on where he wants to take the Mavericks behind young phenom Cooper Flagg and this purchase demonstrates his long-term commitment to the team

#2707. Max Verstappen needs "a conversation" with Red Bull engine after "random" engine braking issues

Ahead of the race weekend at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez – at 2,286 metres above sea level, by far the highest circuit on the Formula 1 calendar – the discussion in the paddock largely revolved around one subject: how much of a challenge Mexico City would pose for the 2026 power units.

Several manufacturers feared severe turbo lag, especially now that the MGU-H is no longer there to support the turbo. The lower air density also raised a crucial question regarding outright performance. At altitude, there are fewer oxygen molecules per cubic metre, meaning the turbo has to work harder to get the same amount of oxygen into the engine as it would at sea level.

Honda chief engineer Shintaro Orihara had already explained on Thursday that if a manufacturer cannot generate sufficient turbo boost at altitude, it would have consequences for the "engine operation condition", in other words, the outright power the internal combustion engine can deliver.

Although this was an unknown for all manufacturers under F1's new regulations, Red Bull Ford Powertrains, as one of the newcomers, was literally facing its first baptism of fire at high altitude.

It was a test that, according to team principal Laurent Mekies, the team passed with flying colours, perhaps even surprisingly so.

"Look, you're right in saying that Mexico is an exception that presents a very, very unique challenge. Power unit wise, obviously it has worked well. So a huge well done and congrats to the guys", Mekies said after Motorsport.com asked him about the power unit challenge at Mexico's altitude.

"Also on the chassis side, it has also worked well, because you have a very large number of challenges on the chassis as well for the car cooling, for the brakes cooling, and for many other things.

"We knew that whatever we were going to see in Mexico would be to be considered as a one-off. We just didn't know if we were going to enjoy a competitive advantage or a competitive disadvantage. But as it turned out, we were in the right mix."

Nevertheless, Max Verstappen believes there are still several areas for improvement with the DM01, Red Bull's first in-house built power unit. One of those is the engine braking. In Austin, this had already given the four-time world champion an inconsistent feeling behind the wheel, and in Mexico Verstappen once again complained about it over the team radio.

"It happens randomly", the Dutchman later explained in the post-race press conference.

"The engine just decides by itself what to do, to be honest, so I don't know. Maybe I need to have a conversation with the engine before going into the race. Maybe it has to behave better", Verstappen joked.

"We don't know, sometimes it just happens. It's not very consistent. But I think everything is running so hot here, also the turbocharger and everything, so it's tough to make everything spot on."

While consistency with engine braking remains an area for improvement, perhaps the biggest positive for Red Bull was that its starts in Mexico were surprisingly good. Both Verstappen and Isack Hadjar had expressed some concerns about them after qualifying, particularly because of the extremely long run to Turn 1, but in practice things turned out much better than feared.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing

According to Mekies, this underlines that Red Bull is steadily making progress with its starts, although he does not want to get carried away just yet. Red Bull's team principal knows that more significant hardware changes will still be needed heading into next season.

"The situation is that we know we are not benchmark. There is a huge amount of work going on in Milton Keynes to improve the starts with what we have this year", Mekies said when asked about the surprisingly strong starts by Motorsport.com.

"And yes, you've seen some of this progress, certainly under high stress conditions today, because we had several starts to make with that very long stretch to Turn 1 where everything is amplified.

"There is a huge amount of pressure and attention around it and I'm very proud of how they managed to give us the best we could today.

"Does it mean we are now the benchmark? No. Does it mean that we will have a perfect start or a start like today in every race? No. But it does mean that we will continue to try and improve with what we have."

#2706. Cardinals workout 7 offensive players

The Arizona Cardinals continue to update their free agent database, and have brought in seven players for a workout on Tuesday. Sometimes, this is just to update, and then again, position groups which are thin will need to evaluate which players to sign to the roster.

All of the players the coaching staff worked out are on the offensive side of the ball.

The players are: QB Carter Bradley, RBs Elijah Tau-Tolliver, Jermar Jefferson, and Ulysses Bentley, and WRs Tyler Johnson, Joseph Manjack, and Jamari Thrash.

Bradley (6'-3", 213 pounds) went undrafted in 2024 after playing for South Alabama where he was named Second Team All-Sun Belt Conference. He then signed with the Las Vegas Raiders and had a good training camp, but was waived on the final cutdown, then signed to the practice squad. He was promoted to the active roster before Week 15 and stayed on the roster for the remaining four games. He did not play any snaps.

Tau-Tolliver was undrafted this year after playing for Michigan State. He signed with the Baltimore Ravens and was a final-day cut. Jefferson was a seventh-round selection by the Detroit Lions in 2021. He played for the Lions for four years and played in nine games. He was injured all of 2022 and was cut before the 2025 season; he signed with the Tennessee Titans, was released, and signed with the Cardinals before Week 5 last year. He also spent time with the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings.

Bentley went undrafted in 2025 after spending his college days at Ole Miss and SMU. He was the AAC Co-Rookie of the Year in 2020 and was named First Team All-AAC. He signed with the Indianapolis Colts, was a last-day cut, signed to the practice squad, and then was elevated to the main roster, then reverted back to the practice squad. This year, he was again a last-day cut, signed to the practice squad, and waived in early September.

Johnson was a fifth-round selection of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2020. As a rookie, he played in 14 games with three starts and scored two touchdowns. He was a final cut after his second training camp and claimed off waivers by the Houston Texans, then released. He had stints with the New York Jets (twice), Buccaneers (again), Raiders, Los Angeles Rams, and Dallas Cowboys.

Manjack went undrafted out of TCU this year. He then signed with the Denver Broncos and was a last day cut.

#2704. FC Bayern trio make FIFPRO shortlist after votes from nearly 20,000 professional players

FIFPRO released 26-player shortlists for both men and women categories ahead of next week's World 11 announcement. The award began in 2005, and it was held in partnership with FIFA between 2009 and 2023.

In addition to the selection of teams in men's and women's professional football, there will be an award for the best players. Despite missing out on winning the Ballon d'Or, Robert Lewandowski won the award in back-to-back years during his time at FC Bayern.

The Rekordmeister have three players in the shortlist for this year's World 11 as FIFPRO unveiled the nominations on Monday based on votes by 19,806 professional men's footballers worldwide. Harry Kane, Dayot Upamecano and Michael Olise will hope to join the previous 11 FC Bayern players who made the final list.

Surprisingly, the reigning Ballon d'Or winner has never made FIFPRO World 11 so far in his career. The striker is expected to rival Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal for the big prize after coming out top in the Ballon d'Or voting. Kane's teammates Manuel Neuer (x4) and Joshua Kimmich made the selection in past years.

#2703. YouTube Gold: The Greatest Players Of The ABA

The ABA lived from 1967 to 1976. It was a short, chaotic, but also exuberant and fantastic era.

The management in the ABA was generally horrible, but there were some brilliant coaches and some unbelievable players.

Julius Erving was, is, and always will be the face of the ABA, but the league had some other immense talents. Guys like David Thompson, Spencer Haywood, Rick Barry (who started in the NBA but spent several years in the upstart league), Connie Hawkins, Dan Issel, Artis Gilmore, George Gervin, and the first great three-point shooter Louie Dampier, come to mind, along with Charlie Scott and Mel Daniels.

This video looks at some of the best players in ABA history.

The league was a race between chaos and brilliance. The merger with the NBA happened in 1976, just in time, because of mismanagement and the lack of a TV contract; the ABA was on borrowed time.

It's really too bad the league couldn't sustain itself, but it changed basketball forever, and its legacy should not be forgotten.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

The Flyers are off to an 0-2-2 start, and the underlying numbers aren't pretty. Per Natural Stat Trick, they have a five-on-five expected goals share of 26.0%, which ranks last in the NHL. Their 4.57 xGA/60 also ranks last. Their 1.94 xGF/60? You guessed it. Last.

Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

#2700. Blow for Lazio as Fans Banned From Traveling for Napoli Clash

The local authorities have issued a travel ban to Lazio fans who were hoping to accompany Gennaro Gattuso's team to Napoli.

This has been a strange year for the Biancocelesti's organised supporters, as they have been refusing to attend the team's home games since the end of January to protest against club president Claudio Lotito. On the contrary, they have been turning up in great numbers at away fixtures, and at times overwhelming the home supporters.

Sadly for Gattuso and his players, they won't be able to rely on the fanbase's support when they travel to Naples this weekend. The shock league leaders will take on Max Allegri's men on Sunday's early kickoff, but the local authorities in Naples have prevented Roman supporters from making the trip, citing public security reasons (via La Lazio Siamo Noi).

This scenario evokes memories of the opening day of the season, when the local authorities in Bologna had initially planned to ban Lazio supporters from travelling to the city, only to backtrack when the Biancocelesti fan groups suggested they could organise a 'cultural' and 'touristic' trip to the Emilian city on matchday, insisting that the authorities cannot prevent them from entering town.

It remains to be seen how the organised Lazio groups will respond to this controversial decision, but a reversal appears unlikely at this relatively late stage.

#2699. Taking stock of the Panthers cornerback room following the firing of Ejiro Evero

Hello CSR! We're coming off a wild week following the most recent Panthers loss to the Packers, one that saw them decide to jettison defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley. It was quite a jarring move to make in the middle of a season where despite a myriad of injuries along the defense, the Panthers still have a shot at the playoffs. As far as the Evero firing goes, I still haven't quite settled on how I feel about it. I think I am currently leaning towards that it makes sense, but probably should have happened following the 2025 season rather than spending the 2026 off-season building around the scheme Evero would use. There were many questionable personnel decisions like not playing 2025 standout UDFA Corey Thornton or 3rd year CB Chau Smith-Wade, along with subbing out some of the younger guys with upside like Princely Umanmielen when the pass rush has struggled. All in all, I think the decision ultimately makes logical sense and I am looking forward to seeing what kind of changes the Panthers make post-Evero to try and right the ship, or at the very least keep it floating with duct tape until they get back Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson, and Jaelan Phillips. The biggest question mark moving forward is going to be what the team does with their depleted CB room. Recently brought back coach and former cornerback DeAngelo Hall will have his work cut out for him. Let's take a look at the current room as it stands.

The 2026 4th round pick became the de facto CB1 following the injuries to Horn and Jackson. He's logged 7 pass deflections in 7 games played and continues to progress after being thrown right into the fire. The Panthers planned on him being heavily involved early, as he manned one of the boundary spots in nickel formations when the cornerback room was fully healthy. Unfortunately, he is day to day right now with a hamstring injury, which means they may miss him for at least a game, possibly more depending on how his recovery goes. Not great, but the experience he's getting this season as a 4th round rookie should prove very valuable from a long term perspective.

The former 5th round pick played quite a bit since his rookie season in 2024. He's played in 36 career games with 11 starts, though curiously his defensive snap counts went down this season following a career high 63% of snaps played on defense in 2025. This season, he's only accounted for 21% of the defensive snaps, playing almost as many snaps on special teams (86) as he has on defense (88). This is a very curious decision considering all of the injuries surrounding this position group. However, that could change this week, especially if Will Lee can't go. The Panthers primarily used Chau as a nickel corner, so prior to Evero's firing, they were playing with additional safeties rather than with as much traditional nickel sets. I think if you're looking to change the fortunes of the secondary, this is the week to throw him out there and see what happens. And that's if they even have a choice pending Will Lee's status.

DeWalt, the final member of the active roster on this list, was brought in on the practice squad on October 24th, and promoted to the active roster ahead of the Packers game last week. He was an undrafted free agent this season, made the 53 man roster for the Atlanta Falcons, but was ultimately waived in October after being a healthy scratch for six games. He made one special teams tackle last week and played no defensive snaps. He played for 3 different colleges prior to entering the NFL, so I don't really know what to expect from him should they be forced to play him this week.

The Panthers (as of this writing, per their team site) have 5 corners on their practice squad. They released Robert Rochell on Tuesday. Most likely, they will be calling up 2 or 3 of them for Sundays game depending on what happens with Will Lee.

The first one I have to highlight is Marco Wilson. He's a former 4th round pick from 2021 who has bounced around the league before landing on the Panthers practice squad on October 6th. He was called on to start against the Packers, being credited with 2 pass deflections and 8 total tackles. Of course, the Panthers defense was still not great in that game as the Packers tore them apart in the passing game, but it was an impressive showing for Wilson and I'd expect him to get called up again and possibly start this week.

Next, we have 2025 UDFA Corey Thornton. Thornton was an impressive preseason story and played in 12 games for the Panthers in 2025, and managed to break in to the corner rotation before a broken fibula ended his season. Curiously, he hasn't been called up at all during the Panthers injury woes from the practice squad. That might change this week depending on what kind of changes the Panthers are making and what options they have for significant playing time.

Rounding out the last of the names is DeVonta Smith, Zion Childress, and Caelen Carson. Smith spent the entire off-season on the roster before being waived during final roster cuts and being added to the practice squad, so he has about as much familiarity as you could ask for from an undrafted rookie. Childress had stints with the Cowboys and Texans since entering as a UDFA in 2025. Carson was drafted in the 5th round pick by the Cowboys in 2024, and has 8 starts in his career. He could very well see some time depending on what decisions the Panthers make during the near future of the post-Evero defense.

In closing, the Panthers have some… interesting decisions to make going into their next few games. It doesn't appear they will be looking for cornerback help outside of the usual roster churning of the NFL season, which makes sense for a team that hasn't made a ton of trades during the season under Dave Canales. I could see a low risk/low price move potentially being made, but dealing a high pick or even mid round pick for a corner doesn't seem to be something they will consider. Personally, I'd really like to see them give Chau Smith-Wade and Corey Thornton some opportunities, and I was impressed with Marco Wilson despite getting thrown out there with less than a month under his belt in this scheme. Caelen Carson could also see some time. But either way, they'll have do a lot of things schematically to mask this weakness currently. They may look to play more man coverage and press to change things up, or they may sit back in the same soft cushion zones we have grown accustomed to. Maybe some calculated aggression in coverage will help?
