#2697. NBA Power Rankings for all 30 teams after opening weeks of new season

So much can change in the NBA in just a couple weeks, and it's already happened to start the 2026-27 season. A massive rash of injuries has decimated the playing field, leaving some teams trying to tread water until their stars return, and others needing to find new solutions with key pieces out for the foreseeable future. No team has been hit harder than the Oklahoma City Thunder, who are missing Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren, and Cason Wallace with long-term injuries that threaten their status as a contender.

Some teams already look dead in the water to start the season, and it's not just perennial doormats like the Sacramento Kings and Chicago Bulls. The Phoenix Suns and Utah Jazz hoped to break into the playoff picture this year, but they've both been just awful to begin this year. Meanwhile, there are a few teams potentially making the jump from good to great who deserve to be taken seriously the rest of the way.

There are some major changes from our last set of power rankings when training camp opened. Let's rank every team in the league so far.

30. Sacramento Kings: One of the wildest stats of the young season is Darius Acuff being tied with Luka Doncic for the league lead in field goal attempts per game so far. Acuff needs to scale back his shot volume and start to get some of his veteran teammates more involved to reach his ceiling, but ultimately nothing is saving this Kings team this year.

29. Los Angeles Clippers: The Clippers just don't have anything they can hang their hat on to start the year. Darius Garland is turning the ball over constantly, Keaton Wagler can't score from two-point range, and there's just not enough size in the front court. This team is bad, bad.

28. Milwaukee Bucks: It was always going to be a long year for the Bucks after the Giannis trade, and it's already proving true. This team is dreadful on both ends despite head coach Taylor Jenkins doing a good job of helping them stay in games to start the year. Tyler Herro has been cooking so far, and his eventual trade deadline deal might be the one thing to look forward to the rest of this season beyond their rookies' development.

27. Chicago Bulls: The good news is that Caleb Wilson has been outstanding, and might already be the team's best player. The bad news is that Matas Buzelis and Josh Giddey are struggling to fit in around the rookie forward, which might put this Bulls' rebuild back to square one around their new franchise player. Chicago's perimeter defense is atrocious, it's not a good rebounding team, and it's dead-last in three-point percentage. It's going to be a long year, but Wilson's activity on both ends is a thrilling sign for the future.

26. Brooklyn Nets: The Nets had five first round draft picks in 2025, and it was immediately obvious that they blew it in the moment. Three of them are fully out of the rotation to start their second season, and even Egor Demin, the best pick of the bunch, is putting up woeful scoring efficiency numbers so far. The Nets owe their pick to the Rockets, too. There's not a lot of hope here.

25. Phoenix Suns: The Suns look dreadful so far, and I'm sorry to say Khaman Maluach, one of my class of 2025 favorites, looks totally out of his depth playing big minutes. The Miles Bridges trade was always going to be a disaster, and it's gotten off to a particularly rough start. I still think Phoenix could be a little more respectable if they would just bench Jalen Green for Collin Gillespie.

24. Utah Jazz: The Jazz aren't supposed to be tanking anymore, but they still look like one of the worst teams in the league. This team has absolutely nothing at center after injuries to Jusuf Nurkic and Jaren Jackson Jr., and the young backcourt of Darryn Peterson and Keyonte George is still struggling to find synergy. At least Ace Bailey looks good to start his second season.

23. Indiana Pacers: The Pacers are trotting out G-League level lineups with injuries decimating the roster. Tyrese Haliburton's return from an Achilles tear was supposed to save this team, but he's immediately out with a hamstring strain, and that's just the start of the injury report. The Pacers just need to do their best to pick up a couple wins until they get their team back.

22. Orlando Magic: Another season, another cursed year of injuries for the Magic. Paolo Banchero and Jalen Suggs are out for the intermediate future, and Franz Wagner hasn't been able to lift the offense by himself with a jump shot that remains broken.

21. Charlotte Hornets: Brandon Miller is off to a hot start, but he's chucking shots as frequently as anyone in the league, and it will be interesting to see how and if that changes when Kon Knuppel and Coby White return.

I was lower than most on the Heat entering the season, but they have still been a huge disappointment regardless of expectations. Klay Thompson looks as washed as I thought he would be, Andrew Wiggins doesn't have enough shooting or creation ability to fit into the new system, and Bam and Giannis still haven't figured out the offensive end. If anyone can solve this puzzle, it's head coach Erik Spoelstra, but the early reports are highly discouraging.

The Pelicans look a little feistier than expected. Zion Williamson is off to a very good start just as the hype around him has died down, Dejounte Murray has helped stabilize the backcourt, and Trey Murphy III continues to be one of the better off-ball scorers in the game. The most exciting development for the Pelicans is that Jeremiah Fears looks better and better every week. This team isn't going anywhere, but at least they're giving their fans something to watch.

The Hawks feel pretty disappointing despite a 4-4 start. Jalen Johnson's scoring efficiency is down and it doesn't feel like he's added anything to his game over the offseason. Lu Dort is showing his limitations on offense without impacting the defense as much as Atlanta hoped. This team doesn't have enough force going to the basket, and the defense isn't anything special despite generating a lot of takeaways and forcing misses from three. The Hawks look mid as always.

The Wizards' terrible rebounding has me a bit skeptical that they can stay afloat, but for now they deserve credit for getting off to a winning start despite integrating a lot of new pieces. Trae Young's passing and foul grifting is keeping his scoring efficiency afloat despite a cold start as a shooter, Anthony Davis is still a very good offensive player who can make an impact defensively when he wants to, and Kyshawn George looks better and better with each passing week. It will be fun to see how they integrate A.J. Dybantsa into the mix now that he's back from injury.

Yaxel Lendeborg mania is sweeping the NBA and reinvigorating the Warriors during the final years of the Steph Curry era. I had Yaxel as a top-5 prospect on my final draft board, so I'm not too surprised by his success, and I tend to believe it will be sustainable going forward. Curry is still sensational when he's able to go, and I like some of the other role players like Brandin Podziemski, Gui Santos, and Georges Niang. It's too bad Kristaps Porzingis is cooked, because I don't know how this team will answer its issues in the middle.

It's not too soon to be worrying about the Nuggets. Nikola Jokic looks like he's lost a step after enduring multiple injuries last season, Cam Johnson is off to another slow start, and the depth of this team is just abysmal. Maybe Jokic will retain his top level and lift everyone else with him, but the Nuggets sure seem like they're going to have a lot of problems if that doesn't happen.

Cooper Flagg looks like a possible MVP candidate in his second season, and that would change everything for the Mavs. The 19-year-old star just doesn't miss mid-range shots anymore, and even if he cools down eventually, his uptick in defensive playmaking is another fantastic sign for his development. Kyrie Irving's return has added another shot creator and pull-up shooter, and role players like Naji Marshall and Daniel Gafford seem more comfortable in their assignments as Flagg and Irving take control of the offensive load. Dallas fans should be feeling good about the direction new head coach Dusty May has the team headed in.

The Knicks just haven't found their offensive stride yet, and they should roar back to form once that happens. Jalen Brunson just isn't hitting shots from anywhere right now, and Mikal Bridges has been ice cold on offense. Backup center was the biggest question for this team after they let Mitchell Robinson go to avoid the second apron, and there has been a noticeable downgrade from him to Andre Drummond. I'm interested to see if they can maintain their status as the league's No. 1 defensive rebounding team. The Knicks will be fine either way.

I may have had the Wolves at No. 1 in these power rankings for a few brief, beautiful days until Anthony Edwards exited the lineup for multiple months with a knee operation. Edwards was playing at an MVP level, and there's plenty of hope the Wolves can regain their place in the title race once he returns. The Wolves feel like they're going to be a pretty inconsistent team until he gets back. Rudy Gobert's offense has been dreadful so far, and LaMelo Ball is running a bit hot and cold as the lead option. Still, players like Ayo Dosunmu and Jaden McDaniels can keep the Wolves in games on the right nights even if Ball is struggling. Minnesota should be able to at least tread water without Ant.

The Cavs have always been defined by their 'core four' in the Donovan Mitchell era, but it does feel like the team made some sneaky moves to improve their depth over the offseason. Mario Hezonja has been a bench contributor who can knock down threes after six years away from the NBA. Meleek Thomas looks like a gem of a second round pick who is adding microwave scoring to keep bench lineups afloat. The Cavs need to get Peyton Watson going, but they should be in the mix all season in the East.

Memphis is the biggest surprise team in the league to start the season. Ty Jerome is playing like an All-Star, and that's actually underselling him because at least so far he'd be in the MVP conversation. Cameron Boozer has been an instant impact rookie as the youngest player in the league despite struggling to score from two-point range so far. Isaiah Stewart has been an excellent addition to the front court with his efficient inside-out scoring and supplemental rim protection, and Cam Spencer and Jaylen Wells both look prepared to take a step forward. I way much higher than consensus on Memphis coming into the year, so I tend to believe their hot start is real even if they're probably playing over their heads a bit right now.

The Raptors still look formidable even with Kawhi Leonard already getting shutdown after two games. Toronto is top-10 in both offensive and defensive efficiency, and they're excellent in the possession game with elite marks in offensive turnover percentage, offensive rebounding percentage, and defensive turnover percentage so far. Scottie Barnes continues to grow as an interior scorer, and if his ice cold outside shot ever comes around, he'll be an easy All-NBA pick. Immanuel Quickley and RJ Barrett have helped pick up the scoring slack without Leonard around, and it will be fascinating to see how they adjust when he returns. One thing to watch: the Raptors are fouling more than any team in the league. When the refs let them be physical, Toronto is hard to beat.

The Blazers' offseason vision is playing out to perfectly to start the season with a team that looks majorly improved offensively while still being excellent on the defensive end. Damian Lillard has hit the ground running as he returns from an Achilles tear, and his partnership with Ja Morant was going a lot better than many expected before Morant exited with a hamstring strain. Deni Avdija is killing it, and at this point has to be considered one of the game's best forwards. Donovan Clingan keeps getting better as a paint defender, and Toumani Camara is one of the league's most efficient scorers so far.

The Thunder got hit with the worst onslaught of injuries in the league just when it seemed like they were the championship favorites. Jalen Williams is probably out of the year, and Cason Wallace and Chet Holmgren are also both set to miss multiple months. The Thunder still have Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, and he continues to play like the best player in the world. Add in an elite defense, and OKC will still have a chance this year even in a diminished state.

The Sixers have a middling offense (No. 19) and a dominant defense (No. 2) out of the gates, just like everyone expected. Yeah, right. Philly has gotten off to a 7-1 start by winning a bunch of close games against a softer schedule so far. The Sixers' defense is benefitting from some poor outside shooting by their opponents, but it's possible that will sustain given all of the attention their collection of stars demands on the other end of the floor. LeBron James looks pretty old to start the year, and Jaylen Brown's scoring has taken a significant step back from 42.2 to 27.5 points per 100 possessions since last year with Boston. I wouldn't be shocked if this team hits a stretch of adversity soon, but it's a good sign that they continue to bank wins. The offense is sure to rise just as the defense is sure to fall, but it should all average out to continue making the Sixers a really good team.

Is this finally the year Luka Doncic wins his first MVP? The 27-year-old is playing as well as anyone in the league, and the team around him makes way more sense than it ever has in Los Angeles. Matisse Thybulle was an inspired free agent signing, and he's giving the Lakers an improved defensive floor while showing his improved outside shooting is no fluke. Walker Kessler has helped the rim protection, which should lift the defense (currently No. 20) when opponents stop being so hot from three. Jake LaRavia also looks more comfortable in his second season. The Lakers are an explosive offensive team with Doncic and Reaves at the controls, and the early returns on the rest of the pieces are encouraging enough so far.

The Celtics still look like the Celtics without Jaylen Brown. Jayson Tatum will be in the MVP mix once he starts shooting better than 23% from three, Paul George has been excellent so far at hitting threes and getting into the passing lanes defensively, and the depth around them continues to be as good as any team in the league. The Celtics' defensive rebounding has fallen from No. 4 to No. 27 since last year. Assuming that's just a small sample size fluke, Boston will continue being one of the best the East has to offer.

The Pistons are proving their playoff crash-out last year has no bearing on their continued regular season success. Detroit is winning with the same formula that led them to 60 victories last year, with the league's No. 1 defense and an offense that's right around league average despite star big man Jalen Durant being sidelined with a hamstring strain. Cade Cunningham is one of the best guards in the league, and Detroit can put a little more spacing around him this year with Duncan Robinson, Kevin Huerter, Isaiah Joe, and even John Collins capable of stretching the floor. Ausar Thompson feels like the best perimeter defender alive, and Paul Reed is proving he's an elite backup big. The Pistons' success last year was no fluke, but ultimately this team will only be judged by its playoff run.

The Spurs haven't looked like the steamroller many expected to start the season, but they still have a top-10 offense and top-5 defense statistically, which is impressive for a team still finding its footing. The three-guard starting lineup with Dylan Harper, De'Aaron Fox, and Stephon Castle has some obvious limitations and may not be built to last all season, but it's still out-scoring teams by +31.3 points per 100 possessions in a small sample. The Spurs have so many different lineup configurations they can go to around Victor Wembanyama, and Julian Champagnie, Devin Vassell, and Tobias Harris (when he gets healthy) are going to factor into high-leverage moments when they need to. The Spurs are far from a lock to make another deep playoff run coming off such a long season, but they still feel like one of the safest bets to be there at the end of the season.

The Rockets look like the most complete team in the NBA through the first two weeks. Houston leads the league in net-rating despite playing the toughest schedule of any team so far. The Rockets' No. 1 ranked offense is probably unsustainable, but there's no doubt that this team has so many more ways to win offensively than they did last season. Alperen Sengun's continued development and the return of point guard Fred VanVleet has helped slot Kevin Durant into a more appropriate role where he doesn't have to create as much. Jabari Smith Jr. looks more comfortable as a shooter, Amen Thompson continues to be an absolute wrecking ball defensively, and Marcus Smart is playing like one of the best value free agent signings of the summer. The Rockets are tough across the positional spectrum defensively, they're great on the glass, and they have more avenues to creating efficient offense this season. At least so far, they look like the best team in basketball.

#2696. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2695. Patriots WR Mack Hollins is expected to practice on Wednesday

The Patriots are set to get one of their top wideouts back at practice on Wednesday.

Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports that Mack Hollins is expected to be back on the field. Hollins has missed the last four games while on injured reserve with a calf injury and a Wednesday return to practice would open a 21-day window for him to practice before he must be activated or shut down for the season.

Hollins can be activated at any point in that window, so he could play as soon as this Sunday against the Packers.

Hollins had 15 catches for 209 yards in New England's first four games this season.

#2694. Week 9 Fantasy Football Mailbag: Should Managers Panic About Ashton Jeanty?

A lot has happened since Week 8 kicked off, and this is a busy time of year for fantasy football managers with the trade deadline approaching and fantasy playoffs already on the horizon. Whether it be the waiver wire, lineup decisions, or trades, fantasy managers are always faced with endless choices to make.

In this week's installment of our fantasy football mailbag, which questions are eating away at managers?

Note: Feel free to reach out to me on Twitter so I can answer your fantasy football questions in future articles.

All stats used in this article are from PFF or Sumer Sports unless stated otherwise. Fantasy rankings and fantasy point totals are courtesy of FantasyPros.

Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty (2) catches a touchdown pass from quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) during the second half against the Los Angeles Rams at Allegiant Stadium. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

One of the biggest Week 8 developments was the Las Vegas Raiders starting rookie Mike Washington Jr. at RB over Ashton Jeanty. Jeanty was limited to just two rushing attempts in the win over the New York Jets, while Washington handled 25 carries.

Although Jeanty still achieved double-digit fantasy points in Week 8, he scored just 10.3 points. Most of those points were due to Jeanty catching 3 passes for 64 yards, and it's tough to expect him to average 20-plus yards per reception moving forward.

There's certainly a chance Jeanty retakes the starting role for the Raiders at some point, but his lack of efficiency as a runner likely led to the change. Among 19 RBs with 100-plus attempts in 2026, Jeanty has the fewest yards per attempt (3.1), the third-fewest yards after contact per attempt (2.67), and the fewest runs of 10-plus yards (5).

Jeanty could still be affected by the injuries he dealt with earlier this season, as he's struggled to display much explosiveness. On a scale of one to five (with five being the highest level of panic), Jeanty is sitting at four on the panic meter.

Baltimore Ravens wide receiver Zay Flowers (4) runs the ball during the first quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals at M&T Bank Stadium. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Things quickly took a turn for the worse for Zay Flowers in Week 8. Lamar Jackson sustained a thumb injury on his first play back since Week 4, and backup Tyler Huntley suffered a toe injury on his first drive replacing Jackson.

As a result of both Jackson and Huntley not returning to Sunday's game against the Buffalo Bills, Flowers finished with zero fantasy points on five targets. Since the Baltimore Ravens' lopsided loss to the Bills, it's been revealed that Jackson is on injured reserve after undergoing thumb surgery, and Huntley will miss the rest of the season with a turf toe injury.

With Joe Fagnano starting for the Ravens on Thursday Night Football in Week 9 against the Jacksonville Jaguars, Flowers should be viewed as a risky WR2 after being a clear WR1 entering Week 8. That being said, I wouldn't bench Flowers unless you have another option on your roster that has a much better matchup or a better offensive environment.

Not only have the Ravens and offensive coordinator Declan Doyle had a week to adjust the game plan around Flowers more, but the Jaguars are permitting the fifth-most schedule-adjusted fantasy points per game to WRs (+5.4). While I could certainly be wrong, I'd still trot out Flowers in Week 9 lineups.

Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) looks to pass against the New York Jets during the fourth quarter at MetLife Stadium. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Throughout the season, I've spoken multiple times about which players fantasy managers should buy low. However, for this week, I'll highlight some sell-high candidates and discuss why managers should move on.

Kirk Cousins is the QB5 in fantasy points per game (20.6), and he tallied a season-high 28.2 fantasy points in Week 8. Despite that being the case, rookie Fernando Mendoza could replace him at any point if he begins to falter.

Tony Pollard has produced 28-plus fantasy points in back-to-back weeks despite playing in a below-average Tennessee Titans offense. Even with Pollard potentially being traded to a better team, it's tough to expect him to continue producing RB1 performances each week.

Rashee Rice could PPR-scam his way to fantasy relevancy still, but the Kansas City Chiefs appear to be on the market for a WR trade. If the Chiefs acquire a notable wideout, Rice would likely see fewer screen passes, and his production is largely dependent on those.

Hopefully everyone's fantasy football squads enjoy plenty of success in Week 9!

#2692. Kane reveals new Bayern deal is "a matter of days" away as Atlético Madrid await

Speaking in tonight's press conference Harry Kane has revealed his contract extension at Bayern Munich may come this week.

“It's a matter of days, not weeks. We had very good talks over the weekend and again today. We are really close now.

“There are just a few details left to iron out,” Kane said as Bayern prepare for Tuesday night's Champions League battle with Atlético Madrid.

“I expect a tough game. It's my first time playing Atlético Madrid, we know what they bring, we know how dangerous they can be in attack.

"We know defensively they can be really solid, really compact, can be tough to break down. They'll be physical and make it tough for us.

“They'll press us, especially in their stadium. So, we have to be ready for a really big battle tomorrow night,” he said regarding the game.

Earlier today, Atlético Madrid and coach Diego Simeone held their press conference in which he praised Kane for his Ballon d'Or win.

“Thank you to Simeone. One of the best coaches there's been in our modern era," the Bayern marksman said in response.

"To have this compliment from someone like him gives me a lot of pride. I think since the Ballon d'Or there's been a great reaction.

"Maybe because my journey is a little bit different to some other Ballon d'Or winners and the hard moments I had to go through.

"Maybe people didn't expect me to reach the levels that I have now, but through hard work and determination and resilience, I've been able to do that.

Of course it'll be a great battle tomorrow night, and I'm sure he'll be doing his best to try and stop me and the team," Kane added.

#2691. Will Wade’s Tigers defeat the Privateers in season debut

It was refreshing to see Will Wade back in action Tuesday night, wearing purple and gold, roaming the sidelines, and even getting a technical foul called during the course of the game. As good as it was to see Wade back on the sideline, it was even more refreshing to see a basketball team showing some promise and ability.

The LSU Tigers defeated LSU New Orleans Privateers, winning 100-57. A few players stood out with some really good performances. Saliou Niang had 14 points, 14 rebounds, 5 assists, and 6 steals. Donavan Dent finished with a team-high 19 points, 10 assists, 2 steals, and 1 block. He also added 4 rebounds. Off the bench, Michael Ruzic, a freshman 7-foot big man, finished with 17 points, 6 rebounds, 2 assists, and 1 block.

This team played pretty well, considering that most of the players had very limited preseason action due to the eligibility issues the team was waiting to resolve. Now that this team gets to play together, the expectation will be for them to continue to grow.

It wasn't pretty the entire game, as the team still committed 12 turnovers and shot only 25% from behind the three-point line. Abdi Bashir was able to showcase his range Tuesday night, finishing 3-of-9 from three-point range and 4-of-11 from the floor, with 11 points off the bench.

Defensively, the Tigers held the Privateers to 25% shooting from the floor and only 14% from three-point range. However, they did allow 14 offensive rebounds, which will need to be addressed going forward. The Tigers also sent the Privateers to the free-throw line 38 times after committing 25 fouls. Expect this to improve as the season moves along and the team gets a better feel for playing together.

This was a really good start for the Tigers. They got the win but still have plenty of work to do. The talent is there, and so are the coaching and leadership. LSU will be back on the court Friday against Texas Southern at 7 p.m. on SECN+.

#2689. Mack Hollins to return to Patriots practice on Wednesday

The New England Patriots' depleted wide receiver group is about to receive a boost.

Mack Hollins, who has missed the last four weeks on injured reserve, will make his return to practice on Wednesday. According to a report by Ian Rapoport of NFL Network, the Patriots will open his 21-day window to rejoin the active roster.

Hollins, 33, was placed on injured reserve following New England's Week 4 win over the Buffalo Bills due to a calf injury. Up until that point, he had played 63% of the team's offensive snaps and been on the receiving end of 15 catches for 209 yards.

His return to practice will be a big step for player and team alike. Hollins is not only a starter-caliber wide receiver and locker room leader for the Patriots, but also was part of a group of three wideouts who recently were forced to miss time. During last Sunday's 24-19 victory over the Miami Dolphins, Hollins was joined on the sidelines by A.J. Brown (knee) and Romeo Doubs (shoulder; IR).

In the three veterans' absence, New England relied on a trio of Efton Chism, Kyle Williams and DeMario Douglas. The trio combined to catch nine passes for 156 yards and a pair of touchdowns in Week 8.

The Patriots will host the Green Bay Packers at Gillette Stadium this week. They will release their first injury report leading up to the Nov. 8 contest on Wednesday afternoon.

#2688. Madrid close in on JJ Gabriel, Man Utd yet to hear from Spanish club

JJ Gabriel is edging closer to joining Real Madrid but Manchester United have yet to be contacted by the Spanish giants or the player's family over the potential move, the Press Association understands.

The teenage talent has been absent from the club since requesting his registration was cancelled in September ahead of turning 16 on October 6.

Gabriel remains registered to United and has been working to get a European Union passport to aid a move abroad, with a switch to Real lined up following interest from some of the continent's biggest clubs.

But the PA understands the Red Devils have not been contacted by the La Liga side or the forward's family over the matter.

Furthermore, United are ready to explore legal options against Gabriel's next club over possible broken regulations.

Real Madrid have been contacted for comment by the PA.

The 16-year-old is the son of former Republic of Ireland international Joe O'Cearuill and last season became the youngest-ever winner of United's Jimmy Murphy Young Player of the Year award.

Gabriel's Instagram account has amassed 839,000 followers and was recently wiped clear of posts, although his recent story updates show him doing individual training.

United had initially hoped to persuade the teenager to stay but it appears his hat-trick against Sabah on his UEFA Youth League debut on September 10 will be his final appearance for the club.

Gabriel shone in the 5-0 victory but his representatives were disappointed he was not registered to play later that day in the Champions League fixtures against the champions of Azerbaijan.

The teenager was due to appear in the League Cup tie against Brighton the following week but had upped sticks by that point.

Gabriel would have become the club's youngest ever player in a competitive match if he had featured in that tie, having appeared off the bench for Michael Carrick's side in the August friendly against Atlético Madrid.

The teenager was included in the first-team team photo published last month and his name listed on the back of Tuesday's Roma programme, despite being left out of the Champions League squad.

United head coach Carrick said on the subject following the Brighton game in September: "I just think we've got to be really careful of the whole situation.

"He's a young boy, he's 15 and the biggest (thing) for me definitely and as a club point of view is looking after our younger players – their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure.

"And I think all of us we've got to be really conscious of that, really, in this situation.

"As a club, for sure, we're all involved in those conversations. I just think we've got to be very careful of that."

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2681. Brewers win the 2026 World Series: Where the Brew Crew ranks among the best recent MLB champions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG -- The Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions. There's so much weight in such a statement on its own, but let's consider for a second all the context behind it.

The 2026 Brewers won 103 games in the regular season and then, more impressively, went a ridiculous 11-2 in the playoffs, never facing elimination, never even trailing in a series. They were one loss away Not only that, but they came so close to being the first team ever to go 8-0 in the League Championship Series and World Series. The 1976 Reds were the only team to sweep both the LCS and World Series, but that only got them to 7-0 because the LCS was five games until 1985. The best playoff record in the era of multiple wild cards was the 2022 Astros at 11-2, and the Brewers have tied that. The 2005 White Sox went 11-1 and so did the 1999 Yankees. We're already up in rarefied air. But there's more.

Think about how hot the Brewers closed. They finished the regular season by winning 15 of their last 18 games. This means they went 26-5 after Sept. 6. Further, look at who they decimated in the playoffs. The Padres were riding a run of 19 wins in 22 games, including a two-game sweep in the Wild Card Series. The Brewers went 3-1 in that NLDS. The Dodgers were the two-time defending champions who swept the Brewers in the NLCS last year. They won 100 games in 2026. The Brewers swept them in four games. The Rays won 98 games in the regular season and were 7-2 thus far in the playoffs. The Brewers took them down in five with their only loss coming in 12 innings.

Remember the Bob Uecker line from "Major League?" There's nothing left but a vapor trail.

That's the Brewers' path to the championship. They just became an absolute killing machine down the stretch, pulverizing everything in their path.

Statistically, they can't touch the 1998 Yankees (114 wins, +309 run differential, 11-2 playoff record including World Series sweep) and certainly can't get to the 1927 Yankees (110-44, +376 run differential, swept World Series). But what about more recently?

Such an exercise is subjective, but let's figure out where these Brewers rank in recent memory. Probably really close to the top, if not all the way up. This wasn't a team loaded with future Hall of Famers, as the Dodgers were last season, for example, but the numbers say these Brewers take a back seat to very few, if any, teams in the past couple of decades.

In fact, let's sort through it. I'll go with the multiple-wild card era, so we're starting in 2012. Let's narrow it down to teams that won at least 100 games and also won the World Series. Yes, the World Series title is a requirement, so we can safely say goodbye to the 2021 Giants and 2022 Dodgers.

We'll compare the teams via regular-season record, run differential, playoff record and how they fared in the World Series. As you'll see, the Brewers will have the most impressive resume here.

An absolute juggernaut in the regular season outside of a wretched stretch before the All-Star break, the Cubs finally broke the faux curse and won it all. They had the regular-season MVP and two Cy Young candidates, in addition to the Cy Young winner from the previous year. On the downside of this argument, they trailed in both the NLCS and World Series (three games to one). Coming back is impressive, but the most dominant teams didn't fall behind.

The first World Series title in franchise history came with a young and (at least it felt like it at the time) fun team. They had the MVP and a former Cy Young winner and also traded for future Hall of Famer Justin Verlander. They needed seven games in both the ALCS and World Series.

The highest win total on the list is right here. They also never faced elimination in the playoffs, though they did trail 1-0 in the ALCS. The MVP of the league was again on the champs and they also had three Cy Young winners (Chris Sale hadn't won his yet, but he was the undisputed ace).

After a 106-win regular season, the Astros steamrolled through the American League side of the bracket, going 7-0. They did lose Games 1 and 3, though, to fall behind 2-1 in the World Series after seeing the Phillies club them for a bunch of home runs in a 7-0 Game 3 win. The Astros righted the ship thereafter, though, and won the next three games, including two nail-biters.

Though the regular seasons are pretty comparable in that chart above, the Brewers were easily the top dog in the postseason. They lost one game between the NLCS and World Series.

We should probably loop in the 2013 Red Sox, the 2015 Royals and the repeat champion 2024-25 Dodgers as well.

If I had to rank them, I think the Mount Rushmore in this era would be:

The 2025 Dodgers were a tough omission, but they didn't even earn a bye due to a relatively low regular-season win total.

I'm willing to hear arguments for the Brewers over that Red Sox team, too. After all, the Red Sox did lose a whole three playoff games, even though they never faced elimination.

The bottom line is that the 2026 Milwaukee Brewers are one of the best, if not the greatest, champions in recent history.

For the first time in franchise history, the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions, and All-Star catcher William Contreras was named World Series MVP. Contreras went 8 for 21 (.381) and drove in four runs in the five-game series. He struck out once. Contreras also went 10 for 14 in ABS challenges behind the plate and 4 for 9 throwing out basestealers.

"I don't have words to say for how I'm feeling," Contreras said through an interpreter following Game 5. "I'm just appreciative of my teammates, appreciative of (manager Pat) Murphy. I want to thank all of them."

"This team's not what it is without this guy," ace reliever Aaron Ashby said after Game 5. "He wants to compete every day. He's our bulldog and we love this dude."

Contreras had plenty of competition for World Series MVP. Ashby threw 5 ⅔ scoreless innings in the series. Jackson Chourio went 11 for 24 (.458) in the series. Rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt went 8 for 19 (.421) and at one point had a hit in four consecutive at-bats spanning Games 4 and 5. All were deserving of World Series MVP honors.

The Brewers acquired Contreras in the three-team Sean Murphy trade with the Atlanta Braves and Oakland Athletics in December 2022. That deal has proven to be a heist for Milwaukee. Contreras has emerged as one of the best catchers in baseball and he's gone to two All-Star Games with the Brewers. Now he's World Series MVP.

Contreras is the first catcher to be named World Series MVP since Salvador Perez with the 2015 Kansas City Royals.

#2679. NBA rumors: Injury-plagued Thunder eyeing player 'they've already had,' and one surging star makes most sense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Last season, a total of 11 players gave the Oklahoma City Thunder at least 900 minutes of service. Three of those players now play for other teams: Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe. Two of them, Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace, have already suffered injuries that may end their seasons. Another, Alex Caruso, has a sprained ankle. For Wednesday's game against the Dallas Mavericks, Chet Holmgren is also out with right knee patellar tendinitis and Ajay Mitchell is questionable with a right ankle sprain.

In other words, most of Oklahoma City's core rotation from a year ago, aside from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, is not available right now. Inevitably, that has sparked quite a bit of speculation. The Thunder are as asset-rich as any team in the NBA. They have the picks to go trade for a difference-maker and a roster spot to add a free agent. The question here is who, and on Wednesday, ESPN's Brian Windhorst stirred the pot with an intentionally cryptic rumor.

"And this is one thing that I've talked to executives about, and I don't mean to be cryptic, but I'm being cryptic," he said on his Hoop Collective podcast. "If you're going to, if they're going to acquire a player, it would not be a surprise if they acquire a player they've already had."

This makes plenty of sense on paper. The Thunder are very particular about their culture. Bringing in someone new is far riskier than reacquiring someone they already know, and given their asset surplus, they can afford to be picky. Given Windhorst's track record of cryptic reporting leading to seismic transactions, let's take a look around the league to see which former Thunder players, if any, make sense as reacquisition targets.

The Thunder traded Dort, Joe and Wiggins last offseason. Given how things have played out, Oklahoma City may regret doing so, and given this rumor cycle, fans will inevitably call for them to try to reacquire one of last season's core pieces. Alas, Dort, Joe and Wiggins are functionally not obtainable to the Thunder. The NBA does not allow teams to reacquire players they have traded until the following season. That means Dort, Joe and Wiggins are off limits for now.

There is a very narrow exception to this rule, but it is not likely to come up. If the player is traded a second time and then gets waived, the original team can re-sign him upon clearing waivers. This happened with Mike Conley and the Minnesota Timberwolves last season. Of course, no team is likely to waive Dort, Joe or Wiggins, so we should assume for the sake of argument that they are off the table.

The Thunder have been so well-run for so long that the NBA is now littered with extremely accomplished Thunder alumni. Of course, these players are, in most cases, either so expensive that they would be impractical for Oklahoma City's purposes or so vital to their existing teams that they likely are not functionally available. So let's roll through those players now:

The players listed above are all currently under contract with teams trying to win today. There are, however, quite a few famous Thunder alumni who are theoretically much more gettable. Four stand out:

A reporter asked general manager Sam Presti on Monday about potentially bringing back retired team legend Russell Westbrook. Presti gave a typical non-answer. Fans would certainly love to see Westbrook in a Thunder uniform again, but the question here is whether he'd be able to accept a small enough role for this to be worthwhile. Westbrook, who announced his retirement in August, is a high-usage player whose value is mostly derived from having the ball in his hands. His issues as a shooter are well-documented, and while he's capable of the sort of intense on-ball defense the Thunder prefer, he's never been consistent as a team defender. All in all, Westbrook is probably just too high-maintenance an addition given what the Thunder could expect out of a 37-year-old.

The point guard Westbrook was once traded for, Chris Paul, makes a bit more sense. He and Gilgeous-Alexander thrived together during the 2019-20 season. However, Paul fell off a cliff during his brief return to the Clippers last season, and he's a notoriously demanding locker-room presence. He's now 41 and has shown no interest in playing in the NBA again after announcing his retirement in February, so we can probably cross him off the list.

Here's a sneaky one: Victor Oladipo. He spent this offseason trying to fight his way back onto an NBA roster. The Sacramento Kings worked him out, but did not sign him. He has not played since the 2022-23 season, but is still only 34. The healthy version of him fit into Oklahoma City's defensive culture, and after several years out of the league, he'd likely be happy with any role the Thunder could offer him.

The only non-guard in this section: Al Horford. The Thunder, again, have plenty of front-court depth. If they did elect to trade one of their bigs for help elsewhere, though, Horford is still useful in a smaller role and the Golden State Warriors simply aren't competitive enough to turn away offers for players in their 40s. The Thunder have several trade exceptions big enough to fit Horford, and his salary is just below the $6.9 million in second-apron space they currently have available.

Any of these three players theoretically could have landed in one of the last two categories. For reasons I'll explain, I wanted to separate them:

George is more expensive than any player we've covered thus far. The only scenario in which this would make sense is one in which the Thunder trade Jalen Williams to Boston (along with a few other contracts, for the sake of legality). That, obviously, is enormously unlikely. It just isn't so crazy that it should be taken off the table altogether. The Celtics already showed a willingness to take a step back this season in the name of the longer view when they traded Jaylen Brown for George in the first place. The Thunder, however, have much more at stake this season given their impending financial cliff. George, with his player option, could actually help on that front by potentially renegotiating a slightly longer deal that suits the Thunder's needs. There would have to be draft picks going to Oklahoma City, and George would have to be willing to take a team-friendly contract that pays him less than Williams is due next season. But if you squint hard enough, you can see something that sort of makes sense here.

The Thunder traded Giddey in part because his shooting made him an iffy off-ball fit next to Gilgeous-Alexander. Well, Giddey has made at least 38% of his catch-and-shoot 3s since coming to Chicago. The Bulls have a new front office that didn't bring Giddey in, and he's struggled to start this season. That doesn't mean they'll give up on him, but it means he could be gettable at the right price. Alas, price is the biggest hurdle here. The Thunder have no obvious way to cobble together the $25 million in tradable salary they'd need to match Giddey's contract without incurring an untenable first-apron hard cap. This would have to be a part of something bigger we can't foresee, so it's unlikely, but if the Thunder do something surprising, there might be a pathway here.

The Thunder could fit him into the trade exception they have leftover from sending out Dort, though they'd have to shed money elsewhere to duck the second apron. Schröder would likely be gettable for second-round picks later in the season (especially if Charlotte rookie Christian Anderson shows he can handle real minutes), and he'd simply be a spare ball-handler on point-of-attack pest defensively. He wouldn't have a big role in Oklahoma City, but the Thunder know him and what he brings to the table. Truthfully, though, the Thunder would probably just prefer to stick with what they have... unless things get worse.

Alright, we've spent the bulk of this story writing about players who wouldn't fit. Let's talk about the players who could. There are two standouts here:

The Thunder ironically chose Dieng one selection ahead of Williams in the 2022 NBA Draft, but Williams outplayed him and Dieng could never find a role in a crowded Thunder rotation. That rotation is less crowded now, especially at forward, and Dieng took advantage of all of the extra playing time he got for the Milwaukee Bucks after the trade deadline last season. Dieng has held a much smaller role for the Bucks this season, so he's theoretically gettable. He can't be traded until Dec. 15 because he just signed a free agent contract, but the Thunder likely don't want to rush into a move anyway.

This is the likeliest big swing on the table for Oklahoma City, if any is even possible. Jerome is in the middle of a breakout season for the Memphis Grizzlies and could be well on his way to an All-Star selection. He's also 29, has serious durability concerns, and is functionally on an expiring contract considering his player option. If the Grizzlies view this as a flash in the pan, or a chance to sell high on someone they don't want to give a big contract to next summer, the Thunder could be their chance. His cap figure is only around $9 million, so he's very obtainable. His shooting makes him an easy fit on any roster, and the Thunder have quite a bit of experience managing the workloads of high-impact players with durability concerns like Alex Caruso.

Jerome is a bit duplicative of Ajay Mitchell, but beggars can't be choosers. If the Thunder have to reorient their roster more around offense to maintain this season's title window, they should do so. Oklahoma City has enough of a draft surplus to trade for even an expensive rental. The question simply comes down to whether or not the Grizzlies view Jerome as a long-term fixture or a pleasant surprise they're willing to cash out. The former is likelier, but we can't rule out the latter.

#2678. MLB Lockout 101: Everything to know about baseball's likely upcoming work stoppage

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 Major League Baseball season is over, and the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions for the first time. The Brewers finished off the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night in Game 5 of the 2026 World Series. MLB Opening Day for 2027 is scheduled for March 24. But whether fans are watching baseball again or not in less than five months is very much up in the air.

Major League Baseball's players and owners are in the process of negotiating a new collective bargaining agreement, or CBA. The CBA is the accord that governs the working relationship between the players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, and the clubs. It covers pretty much every aspect of that relationship that you can imagine, all the way from the overarching salary and payroll structure to daily meal money and days off during the season.

Not surprisingly, it's the economic platform of the game that's the toughest to negotiate because that is always, in essence, a fight over money, or how the league's substantial revenues will be divided up between teams and players. That's keenly relevant right now because players and owners are sparring over whether or not MLB will have a cap on salaries moving forward. The owners have renewed their push for a salary cap after not aggressively (or at least not this aggressively) pursuing one since the 1994-95 players' strike.

Matters are such that the owners are expected to implement a lockout of the players after the current CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year.

There are two kinds of labor stoppages in MLB: the strike and the lockout. A strike is when the labor side – players as represented by their union, in this instance – puts a halt to operations. A lockout is when the management side – team owners and the commissioner's office doing their bidding, in this instance – initiates the stoppage. In plainspoken terms, a strike is a refusal to work, and a lockout is a refusal to permit work to be done. For those on the outside, the result is the same, in that there's no Major League Baseball during a lockout or strike.

When a lockout is in force in MLB, as is expected to be the case after this CBA expires, nothing happens on the major-league front. And we do mean nothing.

There's an almost literal element to a lockout in that anyone on the 40-man roster of any MLB club will be locked out of any team facility for the duration of the stoppage. That also means no access to team trainers or team physicians or members of the coaching staff. Beyond that, there's a transaction freeze in place starting the moment the lockout begins (more on that in a moment).

Additionally, MLB is expected to remove player images and videos from the league's official website, MLB.com, and player images and even names would be removed from articles on MLB.com. A league memo acquired by The Athletic also forbids contact between players and anyone on the club side, at least to the greatest extent possible. The latter extends all the way down to a recommendation against sending holiday cards to players who have been locked out.

Bottom line: A lockout means the sport at the highest level is on hold across all fronts until further notice. "Further notice" almost certainly means when a new CBA is agreed to in principle and then ratified by both sides.

As just noted, a lockout means a transaction freeze, which means no players on any 40-man rosters can be traded and no major-league free agents can be signed for as long as the lockout lasts. Free agency, however, begins on Monday (Nov. 2), so there is roughly one month available for those looking to make trades or signings (once the five-day exclusive negotiating window closes and qualifying offers are extended) before the freeze sets in.

It's worth noting that in the run-up to the last lockout of 2021-22, we saw a swarm of free agent signings just before the lockout began. We could see that flurry of moves again, particularly in light of proposed changes to contract structures that would limit lengths and dollar amounts. Would players like Tarik Skubal, who are eyeing mid-nine-figure contracts, want to get their deals done quickly and hope they're grandfathered in?

That said, there's a lot more uncertainty about what the game's financial structure will look like after this CBA negotiation concludes, at least relative to the last time we did this. That may have a chilling effect on the trade and free agent markets leading up to the lockout date. Clubs don't like mass uncertainty when it comes to making major roster decisions, and they may prefer to see what the league's salary and revenue sharing systems will look like for the next half-decade (the term of each CBA these days) before committing to signings and trades.

If the lockout spans a meaningful amount of time, then that means a great deal of usual winter business will be put on hold. The MLB Winter Meetings and the major-league portion of Rule 5 Draft are typically held in the first half of December, so those could be imperiled. Last time out, the major-league portion of the Rule 5 Draft was indeed canceled, although the November Rule 5 protection deadline had already passed. If the lockout stretches into January, then the exchange of arbitration figures between eligible players and their teams will be delayed. Get well into late January and early February without an agreement, and arbitration hearings and the spring training schedule could be shortened or imperiled altogether. Needless to say, local businesses and elected officials in Florida and Arizona would very much not like that. That, though, could be the least of our worries.

It very well might. It's too soon to say, but there's the real potential for disruption and, perish the thought, maybe even cancellation of the 2027 season. The latter is of course the worst-case scenario, and there's no reason to think there's a strong threat of that possibility, at least this far out. During the last lockout, though, the two sides weren't fighting over quite as much territory, and we very nearly lost games from the regular-season schedule. Lest anyone forget, the last time the owners vigorously pushed for a salary cap, we wound up losing the World Series.

There is a wrinkle of note that may make a worst-case scenario less likely. If the lockout drags on long enough to cancel 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the fallout could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives.

Just players on the 40-player roster will be affected by the lockout, as mentioned. While that includes some minor leaguers, the vast majority of minor-league players are not on the 40 and thus will not be impacted. Minor leaguers now have their own CBA independent of MLB players, and that CBA is still in force. Thus, they're not being locked out. The minor-league season will proceed as normal, albeit minus those prospects on their respective 40s, just as it did during the 2021-22 lockout. So, yes, there will be affiliated professional baseball going on even if the lockout stretches into the 2027 regular season.

To hear commissioner Rob Manfred tell it, the lockout is designed to hasten negotiations between the two sides and speed up the process of forging a new CBA that, assuming it arrives in time, will cover the 2027-31 MLB seasons. Manfred cited this very reason leading up to the lockout of 2021-22, and during the drumbeat phase of this approaching lockout, he said this:

"In a bizarre way, it's actually a positive. There is leverage associated with an offseason lockout, and the process of collective bargaining under the NLRA (National Labor Relations Act) works based on leverage. The great thing about offseason lockouts is the leverage that exists gets applied between the bargaining parties."

After implementing the 2021-22 lockout, Manfred said the drastic decision was designed to "jumpstart the negotiations and get us to an agreement that will allow the season to start on time."

Actions, though, hold sway over words, and after locking out the players, MLB owners didn't make their first CBA proposal to the players for another six weeks or so. In reality, the purpose of a lockout is to preempt a strike. The union can time a strike so as to exert maximum leverage and apply maximum pressure on ownership, say, during the stretch drive or soon after Opening Day or just in advance of the playoffs. From a fan and observer standpoint, though, at least this gets the clock started before games hang directly in the balance.

Yes. The forthcoming lockout will be the 10th labor stoppage in modern MLB history – five strikes and, soon, five lockouts. Here's a quick look at the nine lockouts and strikes that have already happened:

As you can see, there are occasions in which the stoppage is lengthy and disruptive, and in other instances they barely register. Given the complex nature of the current negotiation, the expectation is that the upcoming lockout won't be resolved quickly. There is, though, some runway between "immediate resolution" and "2027 season greatly harmed."

It's the salary cap, first and foremost. MLB has coveted a capped system for decades, but for the MLBPA, the strongest union in sports, a cap is a complete nonstarter. If the stoppage turns into a war, then it will be because owners continue pushing for a cap and players continue to resist. Let it be known that despite the public narrative, the main advantage of a salary cap for owners is not that it will promote competitive balance, but rather that a payroll cap figures to increase franchise values.

Otherwise, changes to the way the league shares local revenues are also up for negotiation. MLB already shares local revenues at significant levels, but Manfred and owners want to share them more equally among teams, perhaps similar to what the NFL does. The good news is that the union has already shown a willingness to discuss such changes and indeed has proposed something similar. That's common ground on a negotiation that figures to need as much of that as possible. As well, increasing the sharing of local revenues, especially local broadcast revenues, would help achieve what the league claims a cap would achieve and do so without a 1994-95 scale of work stoppage.

Given the all-encompassing nature of the CBA, many other issues will need to be sorted out. Those may include the length of the regular season, postseason format, the minimum salary, any changes to free agency and salary arbitration, the implementation of an international draft, retention of the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, draft bonus pools and eligibility, and -- if retained -- the structure of the Competitive Balance Tax system. That's not an exhaustive list, and all of it has to be hammered out, at least in terms broadly agreeable to both sides, for the lockout to end. For now, though, the league hasn't moved off its demand for a cap, and until that changes -- or until the union acquiesces (highly unlikely) -- that issue will determine how long the lockout lasts.

Yes, there is. Once we get into spring training and beyond, any continued shutdown costs clubs and players money. MLB owners have a significantly larger war chest than the players do, but neither side relishes missed broadcast and gate revenues or paychecks. As detailed above, there's heavy incentive to get this resolved before the 60-game mark of the regular season because of broadcast contracts. Along similar lines, with attendance continuing to rise and revenues also increasing each year, the game is in a relatively healthy spot. Pace-of-play initiatives are broadly popular among paying customers, as is the implementation of the ABS challenge system. Expansion to 32 teams is probably also on the horizon. All of that adds up to a potentially lucrative glut of national broadcast contracts, and a lockout that cuts the 2027 season to ribbons would do great harm to what may be MLB's most important business-side objective of all right now. The 1994-95 strike also still provides a roadmap to how much damage the "nuclear" outcome can do to the sport.

Every labor stoppage is a skirmish over money, but the prospect of losing a hunk of the money they're fighting over can reveal shared interests and the foundations of compromise. Therein lies the hope for those of us on the outside.

#2677. Tyrese Haliburton becomes latest injured NBA star: Pacers guard 'week-to-week' with hamstring strain

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tyrese Haliburton's return to the Pacers lineup after missing the entire 2025-26 season with an Achilles tear has hit a speed bump, as the All-Star guard deals with a hamstring strain four games into the year.

Pacers coach Rick Carlisle said Wednesday that after meeting with doctors, Haliburton would be considered "week-to-week" with his hamstring strain and is unlikely to play in the next two weeks.

"It's not good news, but it could be worse," Carlisle told reporters (via the Indianapolis Star).

Haliburton, who sat out all of last season after suffering a torn Achilles in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals, has been terrific for the Pacers in his return to the court, averaging 21.8 points, 9.5 assists and 4.5 rebounds per game on 51.6/37.0/86.7 shooting splits over Indiana's first four games. After hitting some clutch shots in the opener, Haliburton was overcome with emotion thinking about his journey back to the basketball court, and now he will have to find that patience once again as he waits for his hamstring to heal enough to play again.

The Pacers will be without Haliburton for a big game on Wednesday night against the 76ers, with games against the Heat, Nets and Hawks up on the schedule over the next week.

Indiana will try to navigate that stretch not only without their star guard, but with Ivica Zubac and TJ McConnell as players also listed as out on Wednesday's injury report, while Andrew Nembhard is questionable with a neck/back injury.

That's a considerable amount of Indiana's guard depth that either can't play or will be playing at less than 100 percent, along with their top center. That shifts Pascal Siakam back into a lead role offensively and forces the Pacers into more small-ball lineups with Obi Toppin at the five.

For a team trying to get back into the conversation in the Eastern Conference after a lost season in 2025-26, seeing injuries pile up early in the year is extremely frustrating and disheartening. The Pacers were a half of basketball away from winning a championship when Haliburton tore his Achilles in Game 7 against the Thunder and have spent more than a year waiting to get him back to try to make the climb again.

While Carlisle noted in a radio interview on Wednesday morning the hope was Haliburton's hamstring wouldn't be a long-term injury, soft tissue injuries always bring some concern. The Pacers will have to balance patience with the desire to not fall too far behind in a suddenly stacked East.

Haliburton's injury continues a frustrating trend in the early NBA season, which has seen a tremendous number of top players listed on injury reports. The list of stars currently on the shelf with injuries is staggering, with the likes of Anthony Edwards, Jalen Williams, Paolo Banchero, Kawhi Leonard, Jaren Jackson Jr., Chet Holmgren and Alperen Sengun all currently listed out for games on Wednesday night. That's not to mention players like Brandon Ingram, Jimmy Butler, Kon Knueppel and Kristaps Porzingis who have yet to make their season debuts.

While it feels like an absurd number of injuries this early in the season, it's much closer to par for the course than the NBA would probably like to admit. Stars being injured has become a constant concern in recent years, but there isn't an obvious solution.

The NBA schedule is often discussed as a reason for the volume of injuries, but this early in the season, it's hard to point to the wear-and-tear of an 82-game grind. Instead, it feels more like a byproduct of a style of play that pushes players to their limits. The speed of the game is tremendous now and players are pushing their bodies to play faster and more explosively, which raises the potential for injuries.

That's an even harder thing to solve than schedule reform -- which the league and players aren't particularly interested in -- because playing with pace and maximizing possessions is proven to be the most effective style in the modern era.
